speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS BY U.S. SENATE AND HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Order, please. I am sure hon. members will be interested to know that on March 14 concurrent resolutions were introduced in the United States Senate and House of Representatives that the United States Congress extend its congratulations to the parliament of Canada on the occasion of the centennial of Confederation.
The resolutions were introduced in their respective chambers by two great friends of Canada who have long been associated with the Canada-United States interparliamentary group, Senator George D. Aiken of Vermont and Congressman Cornelius J. Gallagher of New Jersey. Senator Aiken and Congressman Gallagher, it should be noted, will once again be the co-chairmen of the United States delegation to the tenth meeting of the Canada-United States group when it meets in Canada next May 10 to 14.
The resolutions were referred on March 14 to the appropriate committees of Congress for due consideration. They have now been reported back and adopted unanimously. The text is as follows:
Whereas the year 1967 marks the centennial of the confederation of Canada; and
Whereas the century of Canadian confederation has been marked by close ties of friendship and association between Canada and the United States; and
Whereas relations have been strengthened through the annual meetings of the legislators of Canada and of the United States: Now, therefore, be it
Resolved by the House of Representatives (the Senate concurring), That the Congress of the United States extends its congratulations and its best wishes to the parliament of Canada on the occasion of the centennial of the confederation of Canada and in affirmation of the affection and friendship of the people of the United States for the people of Canada.
I shall be pleased to convey to the Speaker of the House of Representatives and to the President of the Senate a message of appreciation on behalf of all hon. members.

speechtext:
In the budget last March it was announced that a regulation under the Income Tax Act had been passed to provide that capital assets of certain classes acquired in the period after the date of the budget but before October 1 of this year would be subject to deferred capital cost allowances. This action was intended to serve as a restraint upon capital expenditures at a time when these were increasing at excessive levels.
The present order in council which I am tabling changes from October 1 to April 1 of this year the date at which this period comes to an end. Consequently property acquired after March 31 will not be subject to the deferred capital cost allowances provided for in the regulation last year.
It had been my intention to announce this change in capital cost allowances in speaking on second reading of Bill C-280 because the reason for terminating this period of deferred

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
I wish to inform the house of the support which will be provided by the government to dairy farmers in the 1967-68 support year.


I apologize to my French speaking colleagues: I do not know if the French translation system is working right now. Thank you.

As I am sure hon. members will recall, there is an important structural change in dairy support which will be effective on April
1.	While in past years the management of the program has been the responsibility of the agricultural stabilization board, effective the first of next month the newly formed Canadian Dairy Commission will assume this responsibility. Working with provincial marketing boards this commission has broad powers designed to permit it to develop an industry best suited to Canada's needs.
During the current support year the agricultural stabilization board has provided a subsidy at the rate of 85 cents per hundredweight on manufacturing milk testing 3.5 per cent and an equivalent amount on cream. The estimated cost of this program is $90 million. For the forthcoming year a total of $120 million will be made available to the commission for subsidy payments. This is an increase of 33 J per cent in the level of government aid.
Hear, hear.

This sum will permit of an increase in the subsidy rate to dairy farmers to $1.21 per hundredweight for manufacturing milk testing 3.5 per cent and an equivalent rate on cream. While total returns to producers from subsidy and the market will depend upon the action of provincial boards and agencies in establishing minimum paying prices, I am informed by the commission that the combination of subsidy and price supports will provide for a total milk price in the order of $4.75 f.o.b. the factory for manufacturing milk testing 3.5 per cent.
Hear, hear.

It should be noted that the commission will deduct such sums as they deem necessary for export cost in the same manner as the 10 cents hold back was handled last year by the agricultural stabilization board.
Complete details on the program of the commission will be announced by that body shortly. I can say, however, that it will embody individual subsidy eligibility quotas designed to bring about adjustments aimed at
March 22, 1967

increasing the over-all efficiency of the industry. This, I believe, is a useful step toward the long term goal of the government and the commission to put the industry on a sound basis whereby farmers will obtain a just return for their production with an ever-increasing share coming from the market place.
I should also note that this level of support includes provision for the agreement I reached with the ministers of agriculture of the two major milk producing provinces, Ontario and Quebec, that the federal support, effective April 1, will be increased by the equivalent of 25 cents per hundredweight of milk, subject to the provinces withdrawing from the direct subsidization of manufacturing milk and cream other than in exceptional circumstances. At the same time, since fluid milk is generally accepted as being a provincial responsibility, the federal government will leave the field of fluid milk shippers to the provinces in order to avoid a conflict of jurisdiction.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, this so-called dairy policy announced by the minister today, after his government has been five years in office, will provide very little comfort to the dairy industry of Canada.
Shame.

When we look through the excellent verbiage that has been presented us today what do we find, Mr. Speaker? We find there has been no solution to any of the problems facing the dairy industry. Instead there is an increase in government subsidization, by direct payment to the industry.
Are you against it?

If the government is not aware of it all I can say is that every segment of the agricultural industry knows that subsidies are not a cure. They are just a medicine and don't solve anything. The government appreciates as well as the opposition that this does not meet the needs of the dairy industry, and that the dairy industry will be back again within 12 months for an increased subsidy made necessary by increased expenditures.
The dairy industry made a proposition to the government and outlined the need for a minimum f.o.b. price of $5.10 per hundredweight in order to operate for the season. What we have today is simply $4.75, with 10 23033-905
Dairy Support Policy
cents deducted for export, which leaves $4.65 for the farmers instead of the $5.10 that they need.
I have been asked if I am against this policy. The real test of the policy announced today will be proven in the next year if we find a drastic change as the result of this and other government policies, with too many creameries closing up, too many small dairies being gobbled up, too many valuable herds being dispersed, and too many young men leaving the industry because there is no money in it.
These are the problems which must be solved, and I contend that this weak announcement of increased subsidies will not solve one single problem of the dairy industry. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the government would have been much better advised to follow the lead set by the ministers of agriculture in the two largest dairy producing areas and try to work out a single control of the dairy industry, placing in the hands of the national dairy commission the power to disperse the very small surplus supplies we have in dairying today.
Anyone connected with the dairy industry knows that the surpluses each year vary from one commodity to another, and if our small surpluses were disposed of in external markets the dairy industry would be in a much stronger position to support itself. This is what the dairy industry wants. This is what the consumer wants, not a continuous policy of support each year for the industry from the coffers of the people of this country. The dairy policy announced today by the minister solves no dairy problem. It just gives the government a chance to buy 12 months in time.

Mr. Speaker, it would be an exaggeration to say that the policy put forward by the minister serves no useful purpose. I do not wish to exaggerate the case. The fact remains, however, that while the new policy which has been announced does indicate a measure of increased support and assistance for those engaged in the dairy industry, it really is an improvement of minor degree. I do not think there should be too much dispute on that point.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The minister's statement contains some calculations and figures which are quite difficult to reconcile. The statement indicates that the increase will bring the level of support to $1.21 per hundredweight. When one compares that with the level of support which has been

March 22, 1967
Dairy Support Policy
paid during the last year it seems quite clear that the increase is only in the order of 36 cents or 37 cents per hundredweight, and really does not come out to an increase of 33J per cent as the minister contends.
Representatives and spokesmen of the dairy producers in this country have taken the trouble and the time during the past few weeks to present a solid case to members of this house showing clearly that the present state of the dairy industry is such that unless some substantial policy action is taken by this government there will be a steady deterioration in the industry in the next short while. The number of dairy producers who are willing and able to remain in the industry which produces this vital food commodity is being reduced rather significantly and rapidly. It is only because of the increased productivity per unit that we are able to maintain the level of milk production we have maintained in the past few years.
These are very disquieting times in the agricultural industry as a whole and in the dairy industry in particular. As has been said by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Kent (Ont.), we could have hoped, the people could have hoped, and the dairy producers could have hoped for some more substantial policy announcement on the part of this government and this minister.
While I am on my feet I should like to pose two questions to the minister which really should be asked because there is no indication in the statement in this regard. What intention does the government have with regard to the two features in last year's program which were widely criticized within the dairy industry; that is to say, the provision that the price support shall be paid only on that amount of fluid milk which is in excess of 120 per cent of the quota. I see no reference to that in the policy statement. This has been a very serious shortcoming in this past year's program and is something which should be rectified.
Second, I see no indication in the statement with regard to the negative differential which cream shippers have been receiving in the past year by way of price support. Unless the minister and the government are prepared to take remedial action in these two instances, then this new policy statement is even worse than the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) and I say it is.

Mr. Speaker, the policy the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) has just stated may seem
[Mr. Schreyer.l
generous for some, but it does not at all gratify the hopes of the farmers or dairy producers in Ontario or in Quebec, and even across Canada.
Yesterday we had the opportunity of meeting hundreds of farmers from all over Quebec who were able to state their claims with great logic and common sense which claims are based on facts and real needs in the field of agriculture.
Yesterday the hon. Minister of Agriculture, as well as the members from the province of Quebec, met the representatives of the CFU. The latter asked the minister and the government to grant subsidies or some kind of discount to enable the farmers to get $5 per hundredweight of manufacturing milk, and an extra 10 cents for export costs.
Now, we find that the minister, in his statement, or in the announcement of his dairy policy, offers, in co-operation, or within plans, as he says here:

-I am informed by the commission that the combination of subsidy and price supports will provide for a total milk price in the order of $4.75, f.o.b. the factory-

He says this:

It should be noted that the commission will deduct such sums as they deem necessary for export cost in the same manner as the 10 cent holdback was handled last year by the agricultural stabilization board.

This means, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers will get $4.65 f.o.b. factory, and that is not sure. That is far from the $5.10 asked by the farmers.
Mr. Speaker, I find it completely illogical that the minister, as well as the government and hon. members, especially those from Quebec, should welcome such a policy with regard to the farmers and the dairy producers who make up the most important sector of the Canadian economy. No one seems to mind when millions of dollars are granted for all kinds of things, but it is another matter when it comes to giving satisfaction to all those who make up the most important and useful class in society.
For the farmers, it is felt that $90 million is a huge amount and this year:

For the forthcoming year a total of $120 million will be made available to the commission for subsidy payments.
March 22, 1867



This only means an additional $30 million over last year. Farmers are not getting a fair deal and this policy should have been applied last year.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The government is one year late. The farmers will not be pleased with that dairy policy, and rightly so. They will also be right in blaming their members of parliament who met them several times in the last month or so, and were asked to support their request for $5 per hundredweight for manufacturing milk.
Mr. Speaker, I warn the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) that we are going to do our utmost to see to it that farmers, dairy producers receive a higher subsidy, a better price support than the one the minister now offers them. We feel that there is miserliness in this treatment of farmers, when there is so much generosity shown those who benefit from the labour of farmers.
Yesterday the farmers reminded the minister that a tractor costing $1,200 or $1,400 about ten years ago now sells for $5,000. The farmers' average income is about $2,000 or $2,200 whereas in any industry the average income these days is almost $5,000. It is imperative that farmers command a greater concern of the government and I say that the Minister of Agriculture and the government are not now being fair to the Canadian milk producers particularly to those of the two more populated provinces, Ontario and Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I think the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture again points up the need for a conference of all concerned on the whole question of farm income, such as has been requested by the federation of agriculture. The announcement today presents, as usual, a bare minimum of assistance with no related action concerning costs or prices. As usual we see the agricultural problem of this country tackled industry by industry year by year, so that we have a continual crisis.
The measures will, of course, be of some assistance. They will apply more particularly to Ontario and Quebec than to my own province of British Columbia, where the main dairy industry is concerned with fluid milk although there is manufacturing in the Fraser valley. The clear demarcation of involvement

as between the federal and provincial governments is I think one area that is welcomed in the announcement, because any progress in clearly defining responsibility in this field is appreciated.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we should be remiss in our duty if these supplementary estimates carried without serious words of caution being uttered to the government about the grave situation the agricultural industry finds itself in today. Taking a broad look at the agricultural picture we see many farm papers in western Canada calling for a conference of the agricultural leaders of this country. A conference is urged in order that an agricultural policy may be designed. This is what the farm papers are saying. Strange as it may seem, we have been studying the agriculture estimates in this parliament year after year and the government has been in office for three full years, yet farm papers are asking for a conference to design an agricultural policy. This should appear strange to anyone who is concerned about agriculture.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
A new Minister of Agriculture took office in 1965. One would have expected a definite statement from him with regard to agricultural policy. But none has been forthcoming. He has travelled across the country, particularly to western Canada where he condemned the railways for not moving grain fast enough. But when the opposition urged the government to consider the problems of the grain farmers during the passage of the controversial transport bill the minister did not take part in the debate. He was not even in the house at that time.
A major debate has just taken place on the Bank Act. Three weeks ago the minister went out west and instead of concerning himself about agricultural policy he condemned the banks generally and said they had failed the farmers. This is not quite true. I can honestly say that in the last 20 years the banks have been reasonably good friends of the farmers, though they could have done better. The Bank Act which we passed last night could have been changed so as to improve the farmers' position. Instead of laying down a firm policy which would cover the broad spectrum of agriculture, the minister went out west and condemned the banks. A better course would have been to take part in the debate on the Bank Act, to point out areas in which the banks have failed to help the farming industry, and to seek to improve the bill. But the minister did not take part in the debate. Recently he condemned the businessmen. He would be better engaged if he would lay down the broad outlines of a general policy.

We realize he has tried to bring about an improvement in the dairy industry. Continuing a policy which we had laid down for the establishment of a dairy council for all Canada, he arranged a $4 price for milk. It did not work. We have seen farmers putting cavalcades of tractors on the roads in protest against the milk price which the minister announced. He went out west two or three months ago to speak in Winnipeg at a conference of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. He stated without equivocation that there should be no further subsidies given to the dairy industry. Yet today we have heard the announcement of a further subsidy. This is not a policy which will uplift the industry as a whole.
For some time Canada has been obliged to import butter from New Zealand. Can we stand here as legislators and say we have provided a whole market for our dairy products and an incentive to our farmers to produce the butter to supply our needs? How can the minister say he has brought any benefit yet to the dairy industry when for the first time in 20 years we are obliged to import butter?
We are importing some $800 million worth of agricultural products which could be grown in Canada. If an agricultural conference were held, as has been suggested, certain segments of these imports could be designated as capable of being provided by our own industry here in Canada.
I believe it is about a year and a half ago that the Minister of Agriculture told us 40 per cent of our farms today were providing a good standard of living, 30 per cent were on the verge of making the grade and the other 30 per cent were too small to make a profit and might as well quit. Is this the position he wants Canadian farmers to accept, that 30 per cent of them might as well quit? Is he saying that he has given up hope for them and does not intend to provide them with an incentive to stay in business? I hope not. As the leader and spokesman for the industry the minister must be prepared to lead. Where some farmers feel there is no hope he must provide them with hope. He must give them an incentive and, if necessary, see that they receive adequate prices to enable them to stay in business.
There is no reason why an agricultural land like ours should be importing $800 million worth of agricultural products which can be grown right here in Canada. All we need is
March 22, 19G7

an incentive to produce these products ourselves. For example, when has it ever been stated definitely that sugar beets are a necessity and should be grown here in order to stabilize sugar prices? We cannot allow ourselves to depend entirely on Cuba. In a good year prices will go down but after a bad year prices will skyrocket, as happened recently. I am using this as an example. In the sugar beet industry we should ensure through deficiency payments that 20 per cent of the market is satisfied by the home-grown product. I do not have up to date figures in front of me, but the minister might be able to announce that 25 per cent of the sugar needed by the home market would be home grown.
Over the years 6,000 acres of marginal land in Ontario have fallen into disuse, land which four or five years ago produced fruits and vegetables. Today we are importing these products. Why? Why are we so anxious to get rid of 30 per cent of our farmers? Let us have some leadership. Let us have an agricultural conference which will confirm that the various regions of our country can produce the commodities we Canadians want. It might be argued that all tariffs should be abolished and that we should buy the food we need from the West Indies and from the United States. If this line of thought is carried to its logical conclusion we might just as well sit on our fannies and let the United States feed us. They can do it; they have surpluses. But throughout its history Canada has grown on the basis of its agriculture and it is up to the Minister of Agriculture to lay down a policy which will maintain in this country a strong and independent farming industry.
We know that today beef prices are down, pork prices are down, wheat prices are down. It is all very well for the minister to say he is hoping for an increase in the international wheat price. So far no increase has been achieved. About a year and a half ago the minister stated his belief that the world price should be raised 25 cents. So far nothing has happened. It is all very well for economists to tell us that by 1980 Canada will have to double the number of its cattle. This will not help today, tomorrow or next year. Farmers today are not particularly interested in what will happen in 1980. They want a dollar in their pockets today or tomorrow and if they do not get it they will go out of business. It is the duty of the minister to lay down policy, not to say that 40 per cent of our farmers are making good, that 30 per cent are on the verge and that the other 30 per cent should
Supply-Agriculture
give up. What kind of leadership is this? What kind of incentive is this?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
About a year ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture, "Are you aware of the acute hardship which the agricultural industry faces in hiring help"? He replied, "This is a problem but we are introducing unemployment insurance in the agricultural industry." I said this was not going to help. I told him I had noticed that in middle European countries and even in Great Britain there was a surplus of labour. I asked him to make a special effort to bring farm labour to Canada. At a meeting of the agricultural committee he replied that this was a very interesting thought but he had not really considered it.
I then asked the minister, "Will you consider it? Will you have the immigration authorities go over there and make a special effort? Will you have them advertise the need for farm help in Canada and the possibilities in agriculture?" It is still possible for any immigrant who wants to work in agriculture to come here and later own his own land. That is still possible in western Canada, and I believe it is still possible all across Canada.
Some time ago I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration if some effort would be made in this regard. He said no. The Minister of Agriculture said no. Where is the Minister of Agriculture going? What is he doing? This is what farmers all across Canada are asking. Farm papers continually ask, "What is he doing? Why is he not laying down some policy for agriculture?" It is an amazing thing that a minister who professes to be so concerned about the industry is not in the chamber to see his supplementary estimates pass.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The Minister of
Agriculture goes across Canada telling the farmers that the railroads have failed the farming industry and that the banks have failed the farming industry. Then he goes to Toronto and says that businessmen do not understand the farming industry. He has to do more than talk to convince the farmers that he is really concerned about them.
What has the minister done for the agricultural industry since taking office? Not one solid piece of legislation has come before the house under his sponsorship. By order in council he has announced the formation of a dairy council. That is all, and it still remains to be seen whether that council will do something for the dairy industry. It was founded some nine months ago and established a price of $4 per hundredweight for milk. But that did not work because last summer we saw farm tractors parading on all the highways in eastern Canada.
Today the minister has offered milk producers a bigger slice of the carrot. But is this enough? It is not enough for him to say that he appointed a body to inquire into the farm machinery industry. Will this mean a lowering of farm machinery prices? That is very doubtful. In fact Professor Barber says it is not likely.
It is all very well for the Minister of National Revenue to stand up and say that the Minister of Agriculture does not have to be in the house. Certainly he does not have to be here, but if he wants to convince the farmers that he is concerned about their welfare he should be in the house taking part in this debate and laying down policy. If the minister cannot devise a policy he should call an agricultural conference, something which farm leaders have been seeking. They have told him, "If you cannot form a policy and nail down what Canada should be doing in agriculture, let us help you. We will be at the conference. We will assist you." I hope the minister takes their advice and heeds their warning because never before have we had a minister of agriculture so long in office with the whole industry still asking him, "What is your policy"?

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks as a sequel to those of the member for Acadia. Anyone who has an intimate awareness of what is going on in the

farming industry must admit that very disturbing trends are at work, which have accelerated within the past few years. The Minister of Agriculture has been in office for 18 months and hon. members have a right to expect a greater degree of tangible action by him. Up to now he has succeeded in projecting an image as a sort of Canadian Will Rogers, the image of a man who is aware of the problems that face the farming population. I do not question that he has this awareness, and so it is not too much to expect that by now he should have been able to place some legislation before the house which would show that the government was determined to grapple directly with the major problem of the agricultural industry.
The major problem is still the cost-price relationship and the indices showing the cost-price relationship are readily available. I believe the truth will come out ultimately that during the government's term of office problems within the agricultual industry have increased and its deterioration has accelerated. For example, let us consider the situation with respect to milk production. If it were not for the increased productivity per unit in milk production there would be a very alarming picture simply because the number of people prepared to remain in the dairy industry is decreasing with each passing year.
I wish to make particular reference to cream shippers. Butter supplies in Canada show a pretty clear pattern and one of the reasons why that pattern is at work is that the government's dairy policy actually militates against the cream shipper. I have heard it said, although I suppose it cannot be proven, that the government's policy is a deliberate attempt to ease people out of cream production, reduce the number of creameries and thereby add impetus to the trend toward consolidation of manufacturing plants in larger centres. This kind of policy militates against those smaller dairy producers who are the ones to feel most heavily the cost-price squeeze.
On a number of occasions and again today the Minister of Agriculture was given an opportunity to indicate whether or not the government was going to do anything to get rid of the negative differential in the price support received by the cream shippers. In reply to a question he said there was no differential. But the fact remains that almost every spokesman for the dairy industry has stated without equivocation to members on both
March 22. 1967

sides of the house that the present price support policy results in a negative differential to cream shippers. How can the minister make such a bald-faced statement contrary to the statement made by the organized dairy producers?
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The minister was also asked whether there was any intention to change the basis upon which price support shall be paid on fluid milk surpluses in excess of 120 per cent of the quota. He replied that since this involved fluid milk it was a matter for provincial concern. Yet as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin attempted to point out, almost all surplus fluid milk goes into manufacturing and as a consequence is manufacturing milk when it is in excess of the fluid quota and therefore is properly a matter for concern on the part of the federal Department of Agriculture.
Surely members opposite and the minister are aware that the policy in respect of the payment of price support on fluid surpluses is not very practical at all because it is based only on that amount of surplus which is in excess of 120 per cent of the quota. The end result is that during most months of the year shippers of fluid milk receive support which is marginal and fractional. Certainly it does not amount to anything significant.
With regard to the general agricultural picture, surely the minister and his colleagues must be aware that, despite the unprecedented yields, the net income position of agricultural producers has not improved; in fact it has worsened. Gross income has increased and attempts are being made to point that out. What is not pointed out so consistently is that while gross income has increased so also has the operating expense, the cost of production, and the result is a net income picture which has shown a deterioration in the course of the past few years. What do we get from this government in response to that problem? We see an attitude of indolent nonchalance. The government takes the position that somehow they must depend on the natural market forces. The government refuses to take action in the face of the steadily deteriorating position which faces our agricultural industry.
The result of all this has been a steady exodus from rural areas and farming operations with the result that today, if one looks closely at the situation, one will find that the average age of active farm operators has increased statistically. Behind these statistics, of course, is a very poignant human story. In my own area of eastern Manitoba I have seen
Supp ly-A griculture
conditions develop whereby at the present time the number of farmers below the age of 55 in my home municipality is less than a dozen. One must ask what will happen a few years from now. How will the big transfer of land and production effort from one generation to the next take place? The young people, in the face of the present agricultural income position, are not anxious to take over. Even if the income position were somewhat better than it is, the changing habits of living and working have resulted in many people turning their backs on farming as a possible vocation. It seems evident, therefore, that in order to counteract this kind of development there must be a very substantial improvement in the farm net earnings position.
If I an repeating myself for the fourth or fifth time I do not make any apology because I believe that in respect of this problem there has been absolutely no indication of any concrete or significant action on the part of this government. The minister, of course, as I said earlier, has succeeded in projecting an image of himself as a man of the soil or a kind of Canadian Will Rogers, sort of rurally oriented. He has travelled throughout Canada, particularly western Canada and, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Acadia, has taken swipes at the Canadian Pacific Railway and the banking institutions. If I may use a colloquial expression, he has raised hell with the banks because he alleges that they have not been generous enough in the granting of credit to farmers. Surely the minister is not of the opinion that the farming population of western Canada or anywhere else in Canada is 30 years behind the times and still thinks that it is the banking institutions which are the cause of their present difficulties. Credit is one thing which agriculture has received without too much difficulty within the last few years.
Many persons, as well as myself, have come to the conclusion that the problem is not so much one of agricultural credit as a problem of net income or capital formation. One cannot have capital formation without net income. No matter how much the restrictions on the granting of credit are eased, this will not get at the basic root of the problem unless something is done about the cost-price relationship. In that connection I suppose it is germane to mention that the position taken by the minister in respect of farm machinery prices was quite cute. I use that term advisedly. He let it be understood throughout the country and in the house that he was

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
somewhat chagrined about the pricing policies and practices of the farm machinery manufacturers, so much so that he wrote several letters to them in which he indicated his displeasure. When asked to produce these letters, however, he backed down. He gave some indication to members of the committee that he had received an undertaking from the farm machinery manufacturers that they would not increase their prices during the period when the machinery investigation commission was carrying out its study. He said that during this period they would not increase their prices by more than an average of 3 or 4 per cent. What was not indicated was the nature of this average of 3 or 4 per cent. Is it to be a weighted average?
There is quite a difference between the absolute cost of a tractor and cultivator, and a surflex discer. An increase of 5 per cent in tractor prices and 3 per cent in discer prices is not, for example, a 4 per cent true average. Is the minister talking about an average of the price increases for machinery which has the same relationship as the relationship in using one rabbit and one horse in making a stew? We really have not had an opportunity to question the minister more closely in this regard. It should be pointed out, however, that it is becoming more and more difficult with each passing year to fool the agricultural producers of this country. Now, after the minister has been in office for 18 months and after this government has been in office for four years, reasonable people are saying that it is time some substantial, significant, concrete and tangible action was indicated by this administration. Certainly, if it were only a matter of six months, eight months or one year, the argument could logically be advanced that it takes time to marshall all the facts in order to have a proper base on which to determine policy. But that time has passed and now we should have action. We should have action, as has been clearly indicated already by the hon. member for Acadia and I hope by myself, because the cost price relationship and the net income position have been steadily worsening despite unprecedented yields and increases in productivity.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Where are we going? I am sure the phenomenon of the ever-increasing average age of people on farms in this country is evident in all counties and municipalities across the land, not just in my own province.
It has been my pleasure to have this opportunity to join with other members on this side

to indicate to the government that it has a very serious responsibility which cannot be sloughed off simply by adopting the attitude that because of changing technology and patterns of production a continuing exodus of people from farm lands is inevitable. To what degree should we allow this to happen? If one projects the present trend for perhaps 15 years or two decades one will come to the conclusion that within that time there will only be about 2 per cent of the population on farms. This will likely mean we will have an agricultural industry dominated by vertically integrated, factory type, giant operations and by a few landed aristocrats. Is it our desire to see history repeat itself in this way?
We must also consider the problems in relation to the number of families living on farms with substandard levels of income. I do not oppose the ARDA program but it alone should not be used as a means of coping with the problem of low farm income, and to do so is absurd. ARDA is and will be very useful in dealing with rural poverty as found on small marginal farms, but it is absurd to try to use ARDA to deal with low net income problems facing operators of medium or statistical average even. These people are finding it very difficult to operate at a profit under present economic conditions.
Let me say in conclusion and without apology that up to now the government has displayed an attitude in respect of agricultural problems which can only be described as one of nonchalance, and there can be no excuse for that.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a few minutes of the time allocated for consideration of the first item of the supplementary estimates (G), namely agriculture, to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, that is the announcement of a dairy policy which does not enable producers of manufacturing milk to derive an adequate income from the sale thereof.
WT.en I introduced that motion on the orders of the day earlier, I had hoped to discuss that matter in the presence of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) but I noticed, as pointed out by the spokesman of the Progressive Conservative party a moment ago, that we are forced to discuss matters as important as agriculture and production of manufacturing milk, in the absence of the minister.
March 22, 1967

I know the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) can pilot supplementary estimates, but the fact remains that the Minister of Agriculture is not here to listen to the views of hon. members on the problems of the Canadian dairy industry, particularly in the province of Quebec.
In the last three speeches from the throne, we were told or we have read that the government proposed to give special attention to the agricultural problem, but we have come to realize that the agricultural policy of the government is applied with a dropper. As a matter of fact, only yesterday, many farmers from all parts of the province of Quebec came here, to parliament-some of them had a long journey and even travelled overnight-to meet the Minister of Agriculture and Quebec members of parliament.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I would have preferred to welcome those farmers, those of my riding as well as the others, as visitors, as tourists, in short, as people on holiday. However, to have their rights respected or, at least, to make special representations to the minister, they had to make rather great sacrifices and even to go to some expense. If the Minister of Agriculture and the government had assumed their responsibilities and established a really fair agricultural policy, those people would not have had to come to parliament to demand their rights. They came here, Mr. Chairman, because the situation is urgent, because the situation is alarming.
According to the December 1966 issue of the News Bulletin of the Department of Agriculture, the number of milch-cows, in 1966, reached its lowest level in 46 years. The farmers are getting rid of their herds because they do not pay enough, because they do not bring in the profits the farmers are entitled to.
According to the article, and I quote:
On June 1, there were an estimated 2,279,000 milch-cows on the farm, that is 86,000 less than last year and 6 per cent fewer than in 1961.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, this is one of the alarming aspects or our farm policy with regard to dairy farming. Farmers and dairy producers are justified in being alarmed at such a situation.
The same publication says, a little further on, that:
-the production of manufactured butter has decreased for the fourth consecutive year.
Supply-Agriculture
Mr. Chairman, not so very long ago, Canada produced so much butter that there was a shortage of storage space. I remember that a few years ago, in 1962, 1963 or a little later, a butter warehouse burnt down in Saint-Denis-sur-Richelieu. At that time, the Minister of Agriculture was asked whether Canada and the government would incur a loss on account of that fire. He replied that since it would no longer be necessary to pay storage costs following the fire, it would be so much money saved.
This means then that only a few years ago, the dairy industry did not lag while to-day, for the fourth year in a row, there is a deficit in production, that is to say that less butter is being produced than is being consumed, even with the increased population. In fact, this year, 2,250,000 pounds of butter had to be imported for our consumption.
Mr. Chairman, this is another alarming point of our farm policy and that is why approximately 8,000 farmers were on parliament hill yesterday to demand a fair agricultural policy to allow the necessary profits to which they are entitled, because no one can be expected to continue producing at a loss.
A former minister of agriculture has already said that we should find an incentive other than that of gain to encourage people to produce more. Thousands of Canadians must make a profit in order to continue to produce. How can so many people not understand such an important fact? Since producers cannot make a living, they sell their dairy cattle and abandon their farms, and when they cannot find work in the manufacturing industry or in the services, they become unemployed.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Agriculture and several of his colleagues in the cabinet seem to think that farming has become economically worthwhile in Canada. Yet we know that parishes in agricultural regions are emptying, and that young people no longer want to continue farming well-organized and highly productive farmlands.
Now if there is no one to take over in farming, it is because the operation is not profitable. That is why rural parishes are being abandoned and the land goes to waste. On the other hand, should the farming occupation be a profitable one, we would see the unemployed and labourers leave their cities to take over the farms. Those people would be ready to fight so as to buy land, to

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
make money, but the opposite situation prevails. Farmers desert the land and head for the cities, where they try to earn a living.
That is the present situation. Therefore, I believe that it is up to the government to bring forward, in the dairy industry, a policy which will enable producers to answer the needs of the Canadian consumer.
That is why I blame the hon. Minister of Agriculture for the timid and limited announcement he made earlier and for trying to lead the dairy producers to believe that they would receive $4.75 per hundredweight when, once all the deductions are made they will not get more than $4.10. The hon. minister tells us that the subsidy he offers, that is $1.21 per hundredweight, when the Federation of Dairy Producers asked for at least $1.40, will allow the dairy producers to get $4.75 per hundredweight. Mr. Chairman, that is what the dairy producers asked for last year. The government is one year behind with its dairy policy. That is the reason why the farmers cannot make a profit and ask constantly for a minimum price of $5 per hundredweight for manufacturing milk.

Then, they could make a profit and it could become relatively interesting to be a farmer, a dairy producer and to have herds.
And then, instead of decreasing, our production of consumer goods-which is so important for us-would increase and be sufficient for our national consumption.
We must remember, Mr. Chairman, that when the war was declared in 1939, we had
[Mr. Laprise.l
just got to the end of a depression that had lasted ten years at least. At that time, when it was impossible to sell agricultural products, the farmers were deserting and disorganizing their farms. The hon. member who preceded me stated that the farmers can be assured of a price of $4.75 per hundredweight for manufacturing milk. With this I take issue because nothing has been said about how much is going to be taken off this price, as happened last year, for seeking export markets, and there is really no guarantee at all of $4.75. It is just a hoped for price that will vary across Canada, as was the case last year.
The minister referred to an agreement entered into with the ministers of agriculture for Ontario and Quebec, but I should like to ask about the other provinces. Certainly the policy did not take into account the recommendations, which I have read, made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Most of the thousands of farmers who have ceased operations during the last few years were dairy farmers, which shows that our dairy policy has not solved the problems. The hon. member for Springfield dealt with the discrepancy between the returns to cream shippers and the returns to milk shippers. This in itself is a serious problem. Where do the herds go when dairy farm operations are discontinued? Many of the cattle, especially the better bred, go to the United States and are taken out of production so far as Canada is concerned.
Supply-Agriculture
Speaking of milk shipments 20 per cent over quota, on which no subsidy is paid, may I put this into figures. Let me take a shipper with a quota of 1,000 pounds who ships 1,200 pounds of milk a day. Let us suppose he receives $5 per hundredweight for the first
1,000	pounds and only $3 per hundredweight for the next 200 pounds. This averages out to $4.60 which is less than the $4.75 suggested by the hon. member. And we must also remember that this farmer's costs are higher.
I wonder whether the minister and other members of the house have any idea of the costs of distribution of milk shippers. Do they know what a bulk cooling tank costs? Usually they cost more than $4,000 installed. Do they realize the cost of barn cleaners, silos, equipment needed for harvesting winter feed, the cost of maintaining a high-producing herd, and all the incidental costs of labour, if the farmer is fortunate enough to be able to hire any labour?
The method of paying this subsidy may seem to be a small consideration but over the last year it has become a bone of contention and I hope that this year there will be an improvement. I know this sort of thing can happen in any scheme of this kind, but it should certainly not happen on the scale it has. After a year I am still receiving pleas from dairymen in my area asking me to please find out what has happened to their subsidy. I know that neither the minister nor the department is trying to hold up this money and would not think of doing so. They know it has to be paid and they are glad to pay it.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
But the method of payment is awkward. Surely it should have been straightened out by now. I hope that this year there will not be any trouble with these payments. We should ask ourselves this question: Do we want corporations controlling our agricultural land? maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is a general feeling abroad in Canada that because western Canada had a magnificent crop last year all our agricultural problems have been

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
solved. I want to dispel that idea immediately. There are many spotty districts in northeastern Alberta particularly where crops have been almost non-existent. This has occurred in streaks. It is as though a hail storm had gone through the area, with one farmer obtaining a magnificent crop and another only half a mile away being hailed out, in addition to all the other unfortunate things that can happen to farmers. Northeastern Alberta has been badly hit. Prairie farm assistance inspectors used to be familiar with the districts they worked in and the local problems and they gave relief to the farmers. That has changed. P.F.A. inspections are faulty when the inspectors come from outside the province. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will give this matter his personal attention. The region to which I refer is a designated area.
I suppose that the Minister of Agriculture faces problems with respect to increasing industry in that area, as does the Minister of Industry. I hope that in 1967 these two departments will get together, end interdepartmental competition and let the right hand know what the left hand is doing. Inasmuch as the area is a designated one for industry and a depressed one for agriculture in some places, I ask the ministers involved to get together and work out plans. I know it is difficult for the Minister of Industry or the Minister of Agriculture, both of whom are not from the west, to discuss problems with the representatives of the great prairie area. If they do not wish to accept the recommendations of our own agricultural committee, and we have a fine one, I suggest that they talk to members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and to members of the Alberta Farmers Union, to name two organizations, to find out what the pressing needs of agriculture are in the west.
One way that western farmers can improve their lot, particularly if they have small family farms, is by developing secondary industries in the agricultural field. I can tell the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Industry that the bottleneck in developing secondary agricultural industries is capital. To set up any reasonable industry today takes research, technological know-how and risk capital. The farmers cannot find risk capital. They have not the ability to raise a sum in the neighborhood of $30,000. I suggest that the Minister of Industry get in touch with the Minister of Agriculture to try to work out some formula to meet this need. Perhaps there could be hearings before a government

official of some kind to determine what the local people need. Perhaps they need a rape-seed factory to produce edible oil, perhaps a desiccating factory for alfalfa products, which is a burgeoning industry in Alberta.
The local farmers have not the capital or know how to set up such industries. The Department of Industry talks about disseminating industries among rural communities. The answer is to provide risk capital to get small secondary industries off the ground. That is one area where the government can properly step in, not in the socialistic sense, with help in research and planning by making reasonable amounts of money available. Perhaps the ceiling ought to be $50,000, the money to be made available to local people willing to contribute part of the necessary capital to develop industries which are tied in with agriculture.
Providing aid for research and planning, and also capital, would help all around. Winter employment would be assured. The small family farmer is hard put to pay for the high cost of farm machinery and farm labour. To stay on the farm he must have a secondary industry close to his home. Going to the oil fields or to the bush is not always practical but he can work as a labourer in local secondary industries tied in with agriculture.
If the minister has no faith in the agricultural committee which has made the recommendations I am making time and again, let him listen to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and to the farmers' unions and he will obtain the viewpoint of the farmers. If the minister, together with the Minister of Industry, then makes available the technical know-how and the risk capital we shall take a great step forward in agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on this subject. Everything that can be done must be done to aid agriculture. We hear of the world wide population increase, which many of us have not considered seriously enough. We do not see much evidence of it in this country but it is taking place in the countries of Asia and Africa. While the population of this country remains relatively stable the population of these other countries is increasing rapidly. Half the people do not have enough to eat. This is the stark problem we face today.
An agricultural expert in the United States said the other day that he believes that by 1980 the United States will have no surplus whatsoever of farm products to export. This alarms me in view of the fact that in 1900 the
March 22, 1967

world population was 1.6 billion, by 1920 had advanced to 1.8 billion, by 1940 was 2.3 billion, and in 1965, 25 years later, had reached 3.5 billion.
