maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
An hon. member has said that the pill will take care of the situation. That is probably true in part for Canada which has only a very small part of the world population. The pill will have no effect in Asia and Africa, where two-thirds of the people of the world live, for a good many years. It is expected that the world population will reach six or seven billion by the year 2,000. Fifty per cent of the people in those countries today do not have enough to eat and the types of food they eat are of poor quality. It is natural to suppose that as the living standards of these people improve, and we all hope they will, not only more food but a better type of food will be demanded.
Why is the population increasing so swiftly? The reason is that up to 1900 advances in medical science had not affected the countries of Africa and the Far East. Indeed, they had hardly affected the populations of Europe and North America. Science and medical skill have made it possible for vastly greater numbers of children to survive their first vear-always a dangerous period-to reach adulthood and in turn to reproduce themselves.
What can be done about this situation? Let us look at it. At the turn of this century 75 per cent of the population of Canada worked directly in agriculture. If we look at the picture today we find that the figure is an alarming 10 per cent and would probably be nearer 8 per cent if allowance were made for those working part time or moonlighting. Consider the capital which is required by farmers today. Figures show that for every farm worker in the United States a capital expenditure of $35,000 is involved. In the industrial, field the amount is only $25,000. Here we find a disparity of $10,000 right off the bat. It is obvious that something must be done to help provide capital for those who are engaged in farming.
Once the buying power of the primary producer is interfered with the effect is felt in the urban areas and in the industrial field because the farmer buys trucks, uses farm machinery, uses oil and gas and consumes food himself. He is a taxpayer and he is an
Supply-Agriculture
employer of labour. I often wonder what this country would have done without the billion dollars derived from wheat sales, the largest single item produced by the farmers of this country.
What are the returns which these people reap for the work they do? I find that today there is nowhere in the world, with the exception of the United States, where people are as well and as cheaply fed as Canadians are. I am sure that we as a parliament should take every step open to us, to ensure the continuance of an ample food supply at a price our people can afford. But let us remember that if there are not enough primary producers, somebody else must take over the farms. The position was well set out by one of the leading dairy farmers of Ontario; in fact, he is internationally known. I refer to Mr. George McLaughlin who operates Donrobin Farm near Beaverton. This is what is said about him:
A quiet-spoken, modest-mannered man, looking more like a metropolitan businessman than the operator of the well-known model farm, "Dunro-bin" near Beaverton that he is, made one of the most telling points on behalf of his fellow farmers that the general public has yet heard. Speaking at the annual rural appreciation luncheon of the Rotary Club to a mixed audience of businessmen and farmers, George McLaughlin, noted agriculturist and vice-president of the Dairy Farmers of Canada, noted that Canadians ate better, and at less cost, than any other people on earth.
He pointed out, however, that all this remarkable feat was achieved at the direct expense of the farmer, whose income, in relation to his costs, had declined steadily until it was now 30 per cent lower than it had been in 1949. In the same period, the figure for his fellow worker in industry had risen no less than 54 per cent.
I do not believe the people of Canada generally want this inequality to continue. I do not believe we are that type of people. Mr. McLaughlin went on to point out:
-this spread of 84 per cent represented a subsidization of the economy by the farmer- "the biggest subsidy in Canadian history."
For while Canada prided itself on the low cost and the variety of food offered its consumers, it accorded its agriculture the lowest measure of government support of any country in the western world.
I repeat that statement because I think it is worth noting-"the lowest measure of government support of any country in the western world". Then Mr. McLaughlin says: "The Canadian farmer has been able to survive only through a number of expedients". Money which should have been used for capital purposes has gone to pay current expenses.

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
If we were to visit the farms of Canada today I am sure we would find that the average age of those who are operating them is increasing every year. What is to happen to these farms in the future? Will they be owned by dairies or food processing companies or grocery chains which will be able to set prices at whatever levels they wish and thus obtain the fair return for their labour which has been denied to Canadian farmers?
If the present trend continues we shall lose our export market which has proved a valuable adjunct to our economy in the past. Today we are shipping thousands of Holstein cattle round the world at high prices to increase the value of breeding stock. We possess some of the finest breeding stock in the world and we are proud of it. It has been a lucrative trade and one which has done a tremendous amount to advertise Canada in countries abroad. It has been made possible because our cattle have proved themselves to be of first quality as milk producers and as a source of beef as well.
When I look at the cattle sales advertized in the Holstein-Friesian Journal and in the journals of the other breeds I have grave doubts about the future of this trade. The very man who made the speech to which I have referred, one of the foremost and best known dairy farmers in Canada, is holding a sale this fall and going out of the dairy cattle business. The McCaigues of Glen Afton Farm, Alliston, outstanding second generation breeders, are holding a sale in May. These are people who have built up this flourishing export business from its very foundations with the result that we have been able to sell our cattle throughout the world.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The hon. member for Wetaskawin suggested that the increase in the price for milk was too little. Some hon. members may consider it a fair increase, but really how much of an increase is it when one considers the cost of labour and farm machinery and the disparity between what the farmer is getting and what the man who works in industry is getting? This disparity has brought a man like George McLaughlin to the point where he thinks he can earn a far better living by getting out of the dairy industry. No one doubts that he has ability and it is a fact that he will make a better living outside the industry.
This whole problem strikes right at the roots of Canada because for every farmer who is a primary producer three other people handle his products after they leave the farm.
[Mr. Rynard.l
Not only that, the farmer buys machinery and equipment manufactured by industrial workers in the urban centres. If we are to maintain employment and keep industry viable there must be a better deal for the farmers.
Subsidies are not the answer. They are only a stopgap measure. Parliament and the government will have to come up with a better answer. Something must be done or else we on this continent will suffer from a shortage of food, not to mention the poor people in the Far East and Africa who are improperly fed, with 50 per cent of them underfed at the present time. Farmers must be allowed to reap the rewards of their work. We provide incentives to industry in the form of capital investment in depressed areas and should do the same for the farmer. Food is more essential than machinery or equipment.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity to express my disappointment at the announcement made today by the Minister of Agriculture concerning the subsidy paid to milk producers. My concern is based on the fact that owing to geography many milk producers in my area have to pay more for machinery and machine parts. Their problem is accentuated. I am concerned about the
50,000	milk producers in the province of Quebec. Their industry is dwindling. It is being chipped away and they can foresee its disappearance and the disappearance of their livelihood.
The minister referred to the 33J per cent increase in the total amount of subsidy. This does not impress me because reference to an increase on a percentage basis really does not mean too much. It is applied to the present situation in the industry. We have started off in the wrong direction because even if we paid 50 per cent, 75 per cent or 100 per cent more subsidy it would only mean we would have more people producing milk and selling milk. We have to look at the broader aspect of the whole question to discover how we can do justice to the farmer.
At present the farmer sees the money he has set aside as depreciation on equipment dwindling and eroding. In a few years time he will not have money to replace his equipment. In a few years he will be out of business and his departure will be a grave loss to one of our basic industries.
Unfortunately I could not be here yesterday when the Quebec farmers congregated in Ottawa, because I was undergoing medical treatment in Montreal. However, I feel sorry for them. They were given a build-up which
March 22. 1967

led them to believe they were going to get the price of $5.10 per hundredweight that they sought, the minimum amount on which they can live and secure a fair return for their investment and labour. They have now been let down and let down seriously.
No one in this house need look upon himself as a great defender of the farmer. We are all concerned about the dairy producers and other farmers. We all have to find some means by which we can cure the problem with which they are faced from year to year. In the last three throne speech debates we heard how deeply concerned the government was about the dairy farmer and farmers in general. But all that has been done has been nothing but patchwork. There has been an average increase in the milk subsidy of 10 per cent per year. The increase has done no more than to offset the increased cost of production which in many cases has been more than 10 per cent. The farmer's capital is being eroded and also the money which he has set aside by way of depreciation to replace his equipment. There is danger of the total disappearance of this vital industry.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I believe the increase will be a serious disappointment to all dairy farmers. When I think of all those who are defenders of the dairy producers in the province of Quebec I realize it is not one party alone that is defending them. When the former member for Nicolet-Yamaska was in this house he constantly worried about the dairy producers. In the position he now occupies in his province he is following the same policy of having a deep concern for these producers. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot also expressed concern about the dairy farmer. I do not believe our mandate is being fulfilled when there is an announcement such as that made by the minister today. It will be a serious disappointment to the farmers. It may also contribute to the total disappearance of the dairy industry in this country. How can we cure the problems if all we do is carry out a patchwork job as one would on a pair of trousers? One of these days the trousers will rot away and we will not be able to attach a patch to them.
We should look for other policies. Instead of following the policy of holding farmers to the position they are in today we should look for a policy which will give them the security they need so they will feel equal to those who are engaged in other industries. The farmer
Supply-Agriculture
should be able to receive the same remuneration for his hours of labour as is received by those engaged in other industries. Once we concern ourselves with the problem of seeing that the farmer is equal we will have begun to do something to help bring this industry up to the level of other industries in this country. We have the right to criticize but we also must find a solution to some of these problems. If we followed the practice being carried out by Ontario and Quebec, which have committees to study industries, we would know where the problem lies and would be able to recommend a solution to this problem to the recently created national dairy council. In this way we could start to do something for the dairy farmers of this country. If we were to study this matter properly I am sure we would be able to do something which would bring about an increase in the production of milk. Through an advisory board and researchers we would be able to find outlets for our production.
Because of my concern for the welfare of these farmers I must take exception to the proposal made today by the minister. I do not believe it will advance the welfare of the milk producers. I hope the government will realize immediately that the action they are taking will not be sufficient. I hope the minister and the government will reconsider the policy announced today.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I will forgo for the time being the opportunity to speak.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Lapointe.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to add a few words on this problem which faces the dairy producers at this time, not only those in Quebec and Ontario but all across Canada.
If we remember correctly-and the minister does-the milk producers asked for a minimum of $5 per hundredweight or $5.10, including the 10 cents for the export premium. It is that amount of $5.10 that the Quebec dairy producers asked for officially yesterday when they came 1,000 strong to meet the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) as well as the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, the hon. member for the iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve), and the Minister

March 22. 1967
Supply-A griculture
of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mar-chand) as well as the Quebec members.
Milk producers in the province of Quebec asked the federal government for a subsidy of $1.40 per hundredweight of milk and requested that the price per hundredweight paid by the dairy be raised to $3.60, which made a minimum of $5 in all.
The first thing to be noticed about this request, Mr. Chairman, is that the dairy producers talked of a minimum of $5.10 per hundredweight of milk, whereas last year the farmers received an average-"average" was the word used-$4 per hundredweight of milk. This year, after one year's experience, the farmers are talking of a "minimum" instead of an "average" per hundredweight of milk with a fat content of 3.5 per cent.
The minister did not think it advisable to rectify this first request of the farmers. There is still talk of an "average" instead of a minimum price per hundredweight of milk. We know that after this average price was granted last year, instead of a minimum price, many farmers got $3.70 or $3.75 instead of $4 per hundredweight.
The minister announces an 85 cent raise, bringing the subsidy to $1.21. The farmers had asked for $1.40. But while the minister announces that the subsidy will now be set at $1.20 per hundredweight of milk, the farmer will have to pay 10 cents for exportation, which means that the government subsidy will, in fact, amount to $1.11 per hundredweight of milk with a fat content at 3.5 per cent.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, to continue my remarks on the minister's announcement, the minister says that the Canadian Dairy Commission of recent creation, will be responsible in cooperation with the provincial marketing boards, for making sure that the farmer gets $4.75 when the $1.21 grant is paid.
It might thus be useful to remark that this $4.75 price will not remain stationary. First of all, 10 cents will be taken off for the export premium and, then, the Canadian Dairy Commission will have to get the provincial marketing boards to increase the price of butter, cheese and casein to such a level that dairies can afford to pay farmers $3.54 per hundredweight. Today, we know they give something like $3, and often less-

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Not the dairies. There is no question of dairies here. The hon. member did not understand a thing.
IMr. Grtgoire.]

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, these are dairies or processing plants because some dairies also produce cheese and butter. If they do, then they use what is called manufacturing milk and not fluid milk. But that is another story.
I believe the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) will have to recognize that he does not yet understand the problem. He imagines that dairies do not buy manufacturing milk while in fact many do when, for instance, they make butter, which is what dairies can make or cheese, which they do make and when milk is processed to make ice cream, which dairies do also. Then, dairies use manufacturing milk to transform it into butter, cheese, cream or ice cream.
Then, Mr. Chairman, the dairies or the butter industry, or both, must be able to pay $3.54 per hundredweight for manufacturing milk, plus the subsidy of $1.21 paid by the federal government, totalling $4.75, less the [DOT] 10 cents export premium, that is $4.65.
But who tells us, Mr. Chairman, that provincial marketing boards see to it that $3.54 per hundredweight is paid? There again, the minister does not want to assert it. What is wrong in this whole policy is that there are too many different agencies which can affect the price of the hundredweight of milk.
For instance, if a dairy producer delivers fluid milk to the dairy, that is determined by a quota, and the amount over his quota, less a percentage of 20 per cent will be at the level of manufacturing milk, but for the 20 per cent surplus, the producer does not have a minimum price. If the dairy decides to buy it at $2, $2.25 or $2.50 per hundredweight, the minimum amount received by the farmer for his milk will be reduced by that amount, and that is where the industrial producers, the buyers of fluid milk and the dairies can make their profits.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that there are too many agencies deciding on the prices. There are provincial and federal agencies responsible for the milk delivered by the farmer as fluid or manufacturing milk.
For instance, when the farmer arrives at the dairy to deliver fluid milk, the amount over his quota-incidentally this quota is not always enforced-the surplus of 20 per cent- and even over 20 per cent-for which there is no minimum price policy, does not always yield the support price which should be paid by the dairy.
March 22, 1967

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised that the Minister of Agriculture, who was seconded yesterday by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, as well as several others, could not get the cabinet to agree to $1.50 increase in the subsidy. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) was also one of them. I am surprised that they were unable to get the cabinet to grant $1.40 per hundredweight of milk. Because yesterday, the minister actually told Quebec farmers who came to see him: your latest march will help and support us in bringing your claims before the cabinet and will give more weight to them.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) was also there yesterday. He was much more attentive than today; he is speaking much louder than the standing orders entitle him to do, so that I hear him more than I hear myself. And this has been going on for about 10 minutes.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am surprised to see that the five ministers who were there, after having witnessed that show of force by the Quebec farmers, have not been in position to influence the cabinet to obtain that subsidy of $1.40 per hundredweight of milk. Not long ago, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, the member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), stated that the French Canadian ministers had the right of veto in the cabinet. Nobody disputed that fact.
Finally, there were many French Canadian ministers at the meeting of the C.F.U. yesterday afternoon. They all said and claimed that they would make every effort to help answer the farmers' wishes, namely this $5 per hundredweight of milk. How is it, Mr. Chairman, that those five ministers who attended the meeting, and all those other members who committed themselves to support the case of the farmers before the whole cabinet, did not succeed on their behalf?

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Of course.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that according to the new dairy policy those producers receive an additional $30 million? What is it, if not a gain?

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, of course it is a gain. But the president of the C.F.U.,
Supply-Agriculture
Mr. Sorel, explained to the minister yesterday that in the past farmers obtained a mere pittance, and whenever they did gain anything at all, the cost of living or the production cost would increase even more, so that although they received an additional 15 or 20 cents in subsidies they were not any better off because the cost of milk production rose faster than the prices they could set for their product. That is what the president of the C.F.U. was complaining about. And his argument was very well taken.
Now, this year, to catch up with the cost of living, to permit milk producers to operate at some profit and no longer at a loss, and to enable them to increase their productivity, they will get $5.10 per hundredweight for milk but, in fact, they will barely get $3.65 once they have paid the 10 per cent export premium.
Mr. Chairman, the differential is 45 cents. What they get is not enough to catch up with the rise in the costs of production. And that is important, as was explained yesterday by the president of the C.F.U. who stated that with a grant of less than $5.10 per hundredweight farmers cannot catch up with the costs of production and increase their farms' productivity. Even if they were granted $30 million the increase in production costs was even greater. And that is what should be borne in mind.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Is the hon. member aware that the Livestock Feed Board will soon take up its duties which will be precisely to prevent production costs of mill-feed, for example, to reach a prohibitive level.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman I am quite willing to admit that, and that will likely correct many ills in the future, and that would please me. But, there is something else, this Livestock Feed Board is not operating yet, and the feed prices have already increased. It is a hard fact and this explains the high production cost and why the milk producers are asking $5.10 per hundredweight. If, in the future, it were possible to prevent the feed prices from rising, so much the better; in that case the farmers would not have to keep coming back to parliament to ask for subsidy increases.
Of course, the farmers would be quite satisfied if they no longer had to come to Ottawa to beg for subsidies. But they have to do it, because production costs are rising. And if

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
this increase ever stops, the farmers will be most happy not to have to beg for a raise in the federal subsidies. But the price of feed grain has increased and we are now confronted with the following situation: the commission has perhaps not done its duty in the past, and the price of grain has increased, as well as the price of tractors, of gasoline and production costs. Consequently, the producer of milk now needs $5.10 per hundredweight at least to meet those production costs and to increase his productivity.
This must be settled, Mr. Chairman. And the amount granted today by the minister will not be sufficient to enable farmers and milk producers to meet present conditions, because that small subsidy is lower than the percentage increase of production costs during the past year, and this is serious. Subsidies are not being raised at the same rate as production costs have increased. This was what farmers and milk producers requested and what the government refused.
As I said earlier, I heard the ministers say that they would do everything possible to obtain from the cabinet $5.10 per hundredweight of milk.
We heard last week the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche, state that the French Canadian ministers had the right of veto in the cabinet. Then, could we conclude that the French Canadian ministers have not really pleaded the case of Quebec farmers with the cabinet? It is the Minister of Agriculture who introduced his colleagues from the cabinet to the members of the U.C.C. and, introducing the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) to the farmers, he did not say this: "Now I introduce the Minister of Manpower and Immigration." Not at all. He said this: "I introduce the Quebec leader of our party". That is how he introduced him: "The leader of our political party in Quebec".

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture introduced the Minister of Labour and Immigration as follows: "I introduce now the leader of our party in Quebec."

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Well, then, the Minister of Agriculture says: Since he is the leader of our party in Quebec, he will see to it that the Quebec people get what they ask for. That other minister was introduced as the leader

of the party in Quebec, but obviously it did not mean much because he, with the four other Quebec ministers, plus all the Quebec members, did not succeed in getting what the Quebec milk producers asked for. Obviously, they were not very influential.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Thirty millions, that is a lot.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The member for Lotbiniere says: Thirty millions, that is a lot. Even then, it is not enough to compensate for the increase in production costs on the farm, and that is what counts. Even if you granted subsidies of $40 million, if within the same year production costs went up by $60 million, the farmers would be no better off. That is what the Minister of Agriculture and the member for Lotbiniere must understand. Thirty millions is not an absolute figure; nor is the $5 the farmers are requesting. That figure was based on the increase in production costs, and if it doubles again, $75 million will be needed and not $30 million. The $75 million would not be worth then more than $30 million, since production costs would have absorbed the effect of the $30 million.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Just one question and that will be the last one I ask the hon. member. First, I contest those figures; those are unfounded assertions. However, I ask him this question. Does he not agree that there is not only one level of government that must take action to prevent the rise in the cost of production? Other governments must take their responsibilities.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: This is obvious, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: This matter does not come under the federal government only.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
It is for the federal government to announce the policy on manufacturing milk because it comes under its jurisdiction. The provinces are responsible for fluid milk, the federal government for manufacturing milk. We are now concerned with manufacturing milk because the Quebec minister of agriculture decided to grant a subsidy of 25 cents per hundredweight of manufacturing milk, whereas the federal government asked for this subsidy to be abolished and said: We are going to assume responsibility for what has to do with manufacturing milk. So, the federal Minister of Agriculture assumed responsibility for manufacturing milk on behalf of the federal government. The production
March 22, 1967

cost of manufacturing milk and fluid milk has gone up. And if it did-

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Remember that Quebec increased the sales tax to 8 per cent. The federal government is not to blame.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1967-68 MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Quebec increased its tax by 2 per cent; Ottawa increased its sales tax by 1 per cent. One levies a tax of 8 per cent, the other a tax of 12 per cent. If the hon. member for Lotbiniere wants to pursue this discussion and make of it a matter of petty politics between Quebec and Ottawa, I could follow him on that field. But I will not do it and I will not play politics at the expense of the farmers and the dairy producers. I will leave that to the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
But one thing remains, Mr. Chairman. Even if there is a flaw in the system, even if there are faults in our system on account of which our farmers are caught between two governments and do not know where to go, if our farmers and our dairy producers are taxed by two governments instead of one and if it were better for them to have only one government, and they chose the Quebec government, one thing remains, Mr. Chairman, namely that at the present time we are still living in Canada, that the federal government is taxing the people in Quebec, the dairy farmers like the others, that it has responsibilities towards the dairy producers, that the federal Minister of Agriculture chose to have jurisdiction over manufacturing milk and left to the provinces jurisdiction over fluid milk, the minister should at least fulfill his duties. One of them was to take into consideration the representations made by the representatives of the dairy producers when they were received by the minister and hon. members yesterday on parliament hill.
The dairy farmers came to explain their problems to us in a very simple, clear and concise manner. They said: At the present time, the farmers have the lowest standard of living of all the social classes in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture cannot deny that. The dairy producers said: The farmers' production cost has increased more than that of any other group. The Minister of Agriculture cannot deny that. And the farmers said: What we want is not to become millionaires but at least to be able to face increases in production costs and have a little money to increase the productivity of our land and improve our production. The minister cannot deny that either because he was there when the dairy farmers said it. And the farmers, 23033-907
Supply-Agriculture
the dairy producers said: To reach those objectives we need $5.10 per hundredweight of milk. It seems to me that the reasons given by the president and the vice presidents of the C.F.U. and the president of the Quebec Association of Dairy Producers were clear and convincing. Those farmers came to talk to us not as businessmen but as people who like their farms, their land, their work. They work from early morning until late at night; their income is the lowest although they work the longest hours of all Canadian citizens.
It was moving to hear the president of the Catholic Farmers Union tell us: If we want to make $2,000, $2,200, $2,400 a year, our wives and children must work without pay, and then we have an income which, for one person alone, ranks amongst the lowest in Canada.
Are the farmers' requests exaggerated, Mr. Chairman? Not in the least. They were not asking for extravagant incomes; they were merely asking for enough to live on their farms, before they have to leave them for lack of sufficient income to make a decent living. That is what the farmers came to ask. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Cho-quette) will agree with me that when they asked $5.10 per hundredweight of milk, they were not asking for salaries of $5,000 or $6,000 a year. They were asking for the minimum to allow them to live decently on their farms. The member for Lotbiniere has farmers in his district. Is he going to tell me that $5.10 per hundredweight of milk would make those farmers richer than our city workers? Never. It would give them an even lower standard of living than urban workers, teachers, dealers or other classes of society.
The request of dairy farmers from Lotbiniere country and elsewhere was not excessive. The hon. member for Lotbiniere knows that they were not being unreasonable in asking $5.10 per hundredweight of milk so as to be able to meet their production costs, increase their productivity and modernize their equipment.
When I see those who object to the farmers' claims, when farmers are probably the group which is most neglected by the federal government, and when I make a comparison with federal subsidies for gold production of between $8 and $10 an ounce. The federal government pays from $8 to $10 to gold mines for every ounce of gold produced. This makes $16,000 per hundredweight of gold. Yet, when the farmers ask for $1.40 per

March 22, 1987
Supply-Agriculture
hundredweight of milk, some people rush in to defend the government policy.
I state, Mr. Chairman, that if all of us in this house were to agree unanimously to try at least once, to meet the demands of farmers, whether from Quebec and Ontario or throughout Canada, and give them $5,10 per hundredweight of milk and if we could count on the support of all members approached yesterday by Quebec and Ontario farmers, then, the Minister of Agriculture would have to recognize that this is not an excessive but a minimum demand.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The farmer certainly did not receive the best treatment in the past from either society or the government. I think it is time the Minister of Agriculture thought about that, and I would ask him, Mr. Chairman, to set himself a goal, either in the form of subsidies, by fixing a minimum price for milk, butter, cream, cheese, casein and so forth, or by giving the farmer $5.10 per hundredweight of milk.
I may be told that this would raise the price of milk, butter, and cheese. Well, Mr. Chairman, if the new Canadian Dairy Commission were willing to assume its responsibilities and eliminate all sorts of intermediaries between the milk producer and the retailer, even the savings which would result from this would make it possible to give the farmer $5.10 per hundredweight of milk without raising consumer prices.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to urge the minister to reconsider his position in that respect. And I make a special appeal to all Quebec members who have had the opportunity yesterday to hear valid and convincing arguments from the representatives of the Quebec dairy producers. All those who were there yesterday and who are still here today know that the arguments were most convincing. And all hon. members who are here and who have farmers in their riding, know that the farmers are far from being the class best dealt with by the government, nor the most affluent one.
Well, if we were, for once, unanimous in claiming these $5.10 per hundredweight-I am not speaking of subsidies or anything else;
I am only asking a minimum of $5.10 per hundredweight of milk for the farmers- well, if we were all in agreement on that point, if the Minister of Agriculture and all the members of the cabinet saw that all the members, in every corner of the house, were

unanimously requesting it, I am convinced the cabinet would reconsider the matter and adjust the budget so that farmers would receive $5.10 per hundredweight of milk.
Mr. Chairman, in closing, I am making an appeal for unanimity in this regard. I am convinced the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) is in constant contact with the farmers in his riding. He asked some questions earlier on behalf of his Liberal colleagues. I know he goes and sees the farmers of his riding, that he takes their interests at heart, that he knows their problems and that he really wants-

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to take this opportunity to say a few words about the dairy industry and the announcement made this afternoon by the minister.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we all know that agriculture is in a state of stagnation. In fact, farmers are making representations and putting pressure on the federal parliament, the Quebec parliament and even the parliaments of every province to improve their situation.
The agricultural situation is more serious than we think. Our agriculture is in a dreadful state of stagnation, as those who have eyes can see. If the farmers are taking so many steps, it is because our agriculture is going into bankruptcy. We must make the required efforts if we want to rehabilitate agriculture.
Agriculture must be rehabilitated because it is the foundation of society. It is the very foundation on which rests our whole economy.
So, Mr. Chairman, small measures or small subsidies, dispensed with a dropper, will not solve our agricultural problem.
Once and for all, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance and the whole Canadian economy must get together to rehabilitate agriculture because it is run down, it is stagnating, it can barely survive. The young are leaving the farm, they cannot see any future in it, any way of making a living out of it, the possibility of raising a family. They want to live like the others. They want to have reasonable working hours and nobody can blame them.
Agriculture is in a state of stagnation. In various parishes of my riding, in the past ten years, 70 per cent of the farmers have left their farm.
In one small parish, comprising approximately sixty farmers, 13 farmers left their farm during the same week. This has been happening everywhere for the past several months.
Supply-Agriculture
It can be truly said that agriculture is in a state of stagnation. Farmers are surely justified in expressing their views and in making their plight known to the government.
It is not the fault of the farmers, but of the greatest economic factor, the financial factor. The financial system has driven farmers into debt, together with farm loans.
Farm loans were supposed to save agriculture as a whole, but it was not saved. It was sunk and it floundered. The further ahead we go, the deeper the farmer goes into the hole. This results from several economic factors of our system, which is upside down.
The system has to be corrected. When we talk about reforming the system, we are taken for cranks, for ignorant people, we are taken for people who have never been to university. But why did the intelligent people who went to university bring ruin upon us? Why did they lead us into our present situation, where nobody can live reasonably any more in a country overflowing with wealth?
The problem, Mr. Chairman, is that farmers produce below cost. That is why they need farm loans. When you produce below cost, you can neither repay your loans nor modernize your farm.
When a farmer is given a loan, he is not given enough to turn his farm into an economically worthwhile enterprise. He is given about half of what he needs, or three quarters, and he never gets the balance. And with that, he cannot enlarge his property; he cannot neither improve his land nor his farm buildings; he cannot improve his machinery. He does not have enough of one farm loan, because it is too small.
The farmer who needs $20,000 is loaned $12,000, $13,000, $10,000 approximately. There is one of the problems. If you want to lend money to farmers, if you want to improve agriculture, lend enough to enable it to recover. Or else allow them to make profits, and then farm loans will not be needed! A great number of farmers will then be able to do without the various farm loans or other bank loans granted at excessive interest rates. They had to borrow because they were not making any profit, and the minister knows it.
Therefore, farmers are in a bad way and prices keep going up. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) says the government is doing much for the farmers, but he turned a deaf ear to what was said yesterday,

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
for instance. The farmer needs a lot of equipment: a car, a truck, a tractor and various farm equipment. He also needs buildings and all kinds of materials and implements. The farmer is one of the biggest consumers in Canada, for he needs all sorts of things in various fields.
The farmer keeps on buying things while the government keeps on raising taxes and interest rates. Therefore, the way things are going, economically the farmer is going from bad to worse. When a farmer needs some instruments or materials to improve or build installations, he has to pay the 11 per cent tax, the 12 per cent tax, school and municipal taxes. The cost of living is rising for farmers just as for other people, and their profits are not sufficient to balance all those increases in the cost of living.
I shall not enter into details, knowing that $90 million is considered a prohibitive amount, for farming. Everyone is shocked at the thought we spend billions for defence, feeling it is nothing. And when it is not enough, supplementary budgets are brought down for defence. But when it comes to forming the very foundation of our society, of the economy of the entire nation, we do not move. Subtract $50 million from the $90 million for management, and you will get $40 million for effective assistance to farming. That is what is done for farming, and allegedly it is not possible to do more. It is stated that substantial amounts are given and everything is done for farming, but nothing is done. It is like a drop of water in the ocean. Ninety million.
I suggest that farmers would be better off with nothing at all. They would give up sooner and the government would not be compelled to squander that money with no avail. When funds are invested somewhere, they are supposed to yield profits in the long run, to improve something. But when insufficient funds are granted to improve conditions, it would be better not to give any.
Then, I maintain that the amount asked by farmers, namely, $5.10 per hundredweight of milk, is not too high, that it is not even sufficient. They would need $8 per hundredweight in order to make profits or pay off their debts; it is not with $5 per hundredweight that they will do it.
I say to the minister that within a year, even if he gives the farmers $5 per hundredweight, they will still be in a very difficult position because the cost of living will have continued to rise.

What must be done is to stop the rise in the price of farm equipment and machinery, of building materials and the rise of interest rates. Then, farmers and all other classes of society would enjoy a decent living in such a rich country.
The farmers are ready to produce as much as is needed. But the prices are not adequately balanced. Right now, we find a decline in the budget. A great number of farmers of my area, as everywhere else in the country, have set up an organization to produce pork. And now, as we say, they are played a low trick. Hog prices are down and once again people who made high expenditures can no longer make both ends meet. Anything related to agriculture is discouraged. It is the same in all areas. When the farmer manages to produce beef, the same thing happens. If he manages to produce milk, he faces the same situation. It is the same thing in all agricultural sectors. The farmer cannot even set his price, when he has merchandise to sell, for it is the dealer who comes to him and says: I'll give you so much for your products. The farmer cannot charge his own price, though he knows that the price offered to him is lower than his production cost. He needs money so much that quite often, he sells under cost.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is the government's duty as well as that of the Minister of Agriculture to submit a true master plan, a true reform of agriculture with all the millions of dollars that will be needed to give it the expansion and the vitality which will enable it to play its role and make it possible for the farmers to stay on their land, for those who are qualified to go into farming and do something they like for a living.
Thus, Mr. Chairman, wonders will happen in the field of agriculture and the millions of dollars spent for its development will be counterblanced this time by the millions of dollars which will find their way into the Canadian economy. Today we are not always sure to recuperate the millions of dollars allocated to agriculture because when farmers leave their land they forget about their farm loan at the same time and the governments get stuck with the abandoned land.
One must not imagine, Mr. Chairman, that the Quebec government has not on hand several pieces of land that it has been compelled to take over. Statistics show that very few federal farm loans have been granted in
March 22, 1967

the province of Quebec. There are a few, but, for the most part, the farm loans have been made by the provincial government, since the latter are a little more advantageous than the federal ones. That is why, almost all farmers have taken advantage of the provincial farm loans. But, one should go and see how many pieces of land the provincial government has on hand at this time, because it has been unable to sell them.
When a farmer who has worked all his life to build a farm worth $25,000, $30,000, $40,000 or $50,000, wants to sell his land because he is too old, he cannot even give it away. Then, he has worked all his life for nothing. And that is what the young people refuse to do. That is the reason why the young people do not want to stay on the farms, because farming is in a frightening state of stagnation. We have to get it out of the doldrums and, in order to do that, the hon. minister has a lot of studies to undertake.
Even as individual members, we must assume our responsibility in this house. It is not simply that of the Minister of Agriculture but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), the officials in every department and all the members must assume their responsibilities with regard to what is happening in agriculture, because the conditions are not easy. In fact, the problem is far more serious than we seem to realize.
Mr. Chairman, I shall not say any more, although I would still have quite a lot to say about agriculture. However, I have said enough to show you that farming calls for reform.

Mr. Chairman, may I put a question to the hon. Minister of Agriculture? [DOT] (6:10 p.m.)

I would ask a question of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, could the minister tell me if the price of $4.75 per hundredweight will be a minimum or an average price?

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might take a moment to answer several questions that hon. members have asked.
First of all I wish to commend the hon. member for Simcoe East for his responsible and pertinent speech about the problems of farmers generally across the country, the cost-price squeeze they face and the image
Supply-Agriculture
they sometimes have with those in urban centres. By some it is thought that the farmers are a burden on the rest of the taxpayers or in some way are imposing on the rest of the taxpayers.
The statistics the hon. member drew to our attention were meaningful and pertinent, particularly when one considers that a decade ago the average Canadian spent some 28 per cent of his income on food while today he spends only 20 per cent. That statistic, more clearly than any words of mine, shows that farmers by their productivity and efficiency have contributed to the well-being of the rest of the people. But they have failed to share to as great an extent as other citizens in the booming economy and increasing economic opportunity in our country. All of us concerned with the well-being of the agricultural community must bear this in mind. We must do what we can to improve the lot of the farm community.
When we consider how proud we are of the efficiency of our industrial sector, which in this age of automation and rapidly moving technology has moved ahead extremely quickly, I wonder whether we have paid enough homage to our farmers and to their increased productivity. Statistics I have show that industrial productivity per industrial worker has gone up by approximately 2.6 per cent per annum over the past decade. During the same period the increased productivity of the individual agriculturalist, the individual farmer across the country, has gone up by over 5 per cent per annum, almost twice the increase for industrial workers. The increased productivity of the farmer is the main reason for our higher standard of living. We continue to spend less of our income on food and we have more left over for other amenities, some even the luxuries of life. I thought the hon. member for Simcoe East drew these facts to our attention forcibly.
There is a heavy onus on us, conducting the business of the country in this house, to see that the farmer continues to share equitably in the increased wealth available in this country. The problem is not simple. At the beginning of the second world war about 30 per cent of Canadians were engaged in agriculture. Today only 11 per cent of Canadians are engaged in agricultural production. The economists tell us that within a decade between 5 and 6 per cent of Canadians only will be producing the food for the rest of us. That figure enables us to see the nature of the problem.

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
The agricultural community is becoming more efficient. Production emits are becoming larger. Yet agricultural problems remain grave and difficult. I have found that these problems are not pertinent to Canada only but are generic problems facing the entire agricultural industry. From my studies I have found that the higher the standard of living is in any country, the fewer are the people producing that country's food. All those countries that I have studied, I find, suffer from the inherent problem that fewer, more efficient farmers assume the responsibility for feeding the rest of the population which is moving largely to the cities and the industrial sector. The problem in all these lands is that the farmer receives an inadequate income when it is compared with that of the industrial population. In all countries this is a major concern. Recently it was demonstrated by a major agricultural study undertaken by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development that in countries that were becoming largely industrialized more efficient and larger farm units were feeding the rest of the population.
Mr. Chairman, most of us agree with what the minister is saying, but I express the hope that he is not opening a debate that will take considerable time.
I was hoping the minister would answer my question but he is taking a long detour.

The hon. member for Lapointe thinks he is the only member in this house; he has often left that impression. Many other hon. members have asked questions and it is incumbent on me to try to answer them as best I can.
The hon. member for Acadia raised some points. He complained that I was not in the house for part of the time when he was making his remarks. I think my record of attendance here is certainly the equal of his; in fact, it may be very superior to his. I think the hon. member labours under the impression that, though he is not here very often, if he makes enough noise when he is here he will make up for all those times when he is not here. In point of fact I was in my office attending to a prior appointment. My office is on the second floor. When the hon. member for Acadia speaks one can be anywhere in the building and hear him. One does not have to be actually in the chamber.
[Mr. Greened
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
The hon. member complained about the lack of legislative accomplishment, including agricultural accomplishments, during the past year. Possibly I should clear the record in this regard. He claims that this government has accomplished nothing whatsoever during the past year in agriculture. I would draw attention to the following items. The Farm Credit Corporation Act was amended to increase the capitalization from $24 million to $40 million and to increase the borrowing power from $600 million to $1 billion. An act was passed to establish the Canadian Dairy Commission which I suggest will prove in the future to have been a milestone in Canadian agriculture. Amendments to the Crop Insurance Act were passed increasing the federal level of payment and making the act adaptable to a greater variety of crops. Crop insurance is now available as never before all over Canada. Section 88 of the Bank Act was amended only yesterday to give a very impressive benefit to those engaged in agriculture. I claim no credit for this. The hon. member for Essex South deserves all the credit for it, I believe. But I do suggest that credit should accrue to the government side.
A farm machinery inquiry was established. Hon. members opposite had asked for this for many years and in all fairness I must say that they attempted to do something about it in 1961 and 1962 by bringing this matter before the committee. We instituted an inquiry by highly responsible people so as to allay fears and find new policies in this area. The dairy program in each of the years we have been in office has evolved continuously and shown a continuing improvement. It represents an accomplishment in which I think the government can well take pride.
With regard to the situation in agriculture generally, I think I should point out that for the first time last year farm income in Canada reached a gross figure of $4 billion. Some hon. members opposite including, I believe, the hon. member for Acadia, have indicated that farming is a diminishing industry. Some said that farmers were almost going out of business. Let me cite a few statistics. In the years from 1959 to 1963 the average production of Cheddar cheese amounted to 118.7 million pounds. In 1964 it was 144.6 million pounds, in 1965, 158 million pounds, and in 1966 an estimated 167 million pounds. So there has been an increase each year. What are the figures for cheddar cheese exports? From 1959 to 1963 the average was 21.9
March 22, 1967

million pounds. In 1964 they amounted to 30.3 million pounds, in 1965 31.6 million pounds, and in 1966 an estimated 35 million pounds.
What about butter?

I will come to butter. It is doing fine too. What about the price of beef about which some hon. members from the west should be concerned? Despite their lamentations and their accusations that the government has done nothing, the figures are interesting. The price of beef when they were in office in 1963 was $23.65 per hundredweight for good steers at Toronto on the basis of monthly and yearly averages. In 1964 it was $22.70. In 1965 the price was $24, in 1966 it was $26.03, in January of 1967, $27.50 and in February it was $27.50. I suggest these are improvements and that it is completely irresponsible to say there have been no improvements in the industry. These improvements have been made since we came to office.
What about eggs? In 1963 the price was 34 cents a dozen. In 1966, the average price for all grades was 40 cents a dozen. I will admit that at the present time, as some hon. members have pointed out, there are problems in connection with the supply of eggs. But I think these will be solved as the season proceeds. Even now the price is 35 cents a dozen.
What about wheat sales and wheat products? No less than 840 million bushels of wheat were produced and 600 million bushels went into export. I have a speech made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, formerly minister of agriculture, during his term of office. In it he stated that we should not foresee export sales in the future greater than 300 million bushels. This was quoted in the Western Producer and I am pleased to say I have a copy which I can show at any time to hon. members who are interested. This was the "doom and gloom" philosophy with respect to agriculture which has not been borne out under the authority of this administration.
Someone asked about dairy products. Let me cite a few statistics in this regard. Milk production in 1957 amounted to 17 billion pounds. For succeeding years the figures were as follows, in billions of pounds: 1958, 17.7; 1959, 17.6; 1960, 17.7; 1961, 18.3; 1962, 18.4; 1963, 18.4; 1964, 18.5; 1965, 18.3. Dairy milk used went up in every area except that of farm use where, of course, it has a lower commercial value. In 1952 fluid milk production amounted to 5,117 million pounds and in
Supp ly-A gricul ture
1966 to 5,240 million pounds. Butter production rose from 7,099 million pounds to 7,440 million pounds in 1966 and cheese from 1,212 million to 2,039 million pounds.
I could continue reading figures into the record from now until midnight to show not only increased productivity in agriculture but an improvement in the price structure during the past three years since the government took office.
May I ask the minister a question? Is he suggesting by these figures that the net income of farmers increased in those years?
Is the minister trying to talk out these estimates?

Hon. gentlemen opposite are very prone to make speeches on the estimates which are devoid of substance and contrary to the facts under the assumption that they will get away with it and that no one will show them to be false.
Hear, hear.
If the minister opens this up he will be kept here until after Easter.
This is all right by me. This is what we are here to do, and every time false facts are placed on the record I think any hon. member has the right to correct them.
I suggest the minister should get in touch with the President of the Treasury Board and see what that minister thinks of the way in which he is conducting himself.
If the hon. member is saying it is the duty of members of this house to leave false facts on the record I will be very pleased to take his opinion in this regard.
I do not think the minister has yet answered my question, though it was I who asked him a question originally.

If the hon. member will permit me to finish my speech I will answer questions thereafter.
Some comment has been made about dairy prices. I do not pretend for a moment that we have achieved during three years in office all we would like to achieve. But with respect to the allegations made this afternoon that there has been no progress I think it is fair to point out that when we came to office the price of manufacturing milk was $2.66.

March 22, 1967
Supply-A griculture
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The party that was responsible for a price of $2.66 for manufacturing milk is claiming today that an increase in that price to $4.75 over a period of three years is not a notable accomplishment. The hon. member for Gaspe said, and I took down his words verbatim, "What is a 33J per cent increase"? In other words, what is an increase of $30 million? At one time in this house someone is supposed to have said, "What's a million"? Now we have the statement, "What's $30 million"?
There are improvements in other areas, Mr. Chairman, that I think I should put on the record. In 1961 the total wheat crop was 283.4 million bushels, in 1962, 565.6 million bushels, in 1963, 723.4 million bushels; in 1964, 600.4 millions bushels, in 1965, 648.9 million bushels, and in 1966, 844.4 million bushels. Exports of wheat in 1961 totalled 305.3 million bushels, in 1962, 474.4 million bushels, in 1963, 565.9 million bushels, in 1964, 531.7 million bushels, and in 1965, 566.5 million bushels. Here are the figures of total farm production in millions of dollars. In 1961 the figure was $485.3 million, in 1962 $941.4, in 1963 $1,259.2 and in 1964, the last year for which we have figures, $957.2 million. The price for No. 1 Northern wheat at the lakehead in 1961 was $1.90 per bushel, in 1962 $1.96, in 1963 $2.03, in 1964 $1.98, in 1965 $2.00, and in 1966, estimated to date, $2.11.
If these figures indicate a declining industry-
May I ask a question?

When I finish my speech. If these figures indicate a declining industry, and I know figures do not always tell the truth, it seems a strange conclusion to draw. All these figures in every facet of the agricultural industry show that the industry is a productive one, that the Canadian farmer is doing a tremendous job of production, something which seems to be denied in speeches made from the opposite benches. Speeches made by hon. members opposite indicated that the industry was a dying one, that it was in terrible shape, and some of the speeches indicated that we are going to be out of farming altogether in Canada soon. I do not think we serve the farmers well, or anyone else well, by raising bogies that do not exist, by alleging facts that are not so, or by indicating problems that in fact are merely indicated for political and partisan purposes.

I think we should all agree, as I said at the outset, that we want to do everything we can to improve the farmers' position, that we want to have policies which will enable the agricultural sector to have a better way of life and income more comparable with the industrial sector. But I think we will achieve those ends much more effectively if we face the facts as they are and not as we would like them to be for political or partisan purpose
Some questions were asked with respect to the dairy program. First of all allusions were made, again I believe by the hon. member for Gaspe, to the effect that we gave an undertaking to the very good meeting of agriculturalists from l'Union Catholique de Cul-tivateurs of the province of Quebec who came here yesterday. This was a meeting called at their request. They came here in order to give us their views and to make their representations with respect to the dairy program for the ensuing year.
Those representations were made forcibly but responsibly. Their views were made known very clearly to us. No undertaking whatsoever was given except that the representations which had been made would be given every consideration in this year's program in the light of the government's responsibility. As with this and other programs I do not claim we have achieved everything we would like to do. I do not think we have perfection by any means but I say that a contribution of a further $30 million is a responsible contribution. I say that a program which increases the support at the federal level beyond last year's price at this time of $4.10 to $4.75 is a step in the right direction even though it may not be all we would have it be.
I know that the party of hon. gentlemen opposite has had the responsibility of office from time to time and that its members realize some of the differences between opposition and the responsibilities of government, with the government having to consider all facets and factors of the economy. Members of other parties have never had the responsibility of government and never will have it. The public does not think they ever will have it and so it is very easy for them to say, "You should give everybody everything they want." If we had given everybody everything they wanted by acceding to the requests made from time to time from various parts of the house, this country would have been bankrupt long ago.
March 22, 19G7

Some hon. members remind me of the American congressman who was asked how he stayed in office so long. He said, "I voted for all expenditures and against all taxes." I think maybe there are members of this house and parties in this house that subscribe to the same irresponsibility.
I merely say, Mr. Chairman, that all these facts and figures indicate that the government has created a climate and has passed legislation which has moved the agricultural economy ahead productively and economically. I agree that there is a great deal more to be done, that none of us should cease in our endeavour to bring the farmer into the economic sunlight in the same measure as the industrial worker has come into it over the past few years. But I do suggest that to load the record of this house under any pretext, be it interim supply or otherwise, with facts that are not borne out by the record does no service to the farmer and does not bring the day closer when we will have the kind of comprehensive policies which will achieve the economic results that I think all members want for the agricultural community.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, the minister quoted figures relating to increased production and prices. Could he give us the same prices with regard to production costs? Could he tell us, for instance, how much it cost in 1958, 1959, 1960, 1961, 1962, 1963, 1964, 1965, 1966 to produce a hundredweight of milk compared to today?
I also want the minister to answer my earlier question. Is $4.75 per hundredweight of milk an average or a minimum price?

Mr. Chairman, costs of course depend upon the efficiency of the farmer, the size of his operation and the techniques he uses. I have no cost figures which would apply to each and every individual farmer. I certainly appreciate the fact that the farmer's costs have gone up, that he is caught in the cost-price squeeze and at the same time in some areas is unable to get a better price for his product, but there is one area in which he has certainly been able to get a better price for his product, thanks to this government's policy, and that is in the area of manufacturing milk. However much his costs have gone up I suggest I am very safe in saying they have not gone up during the last three years 23033-908
Supply-Agriculture
in the proportion of $2.66 to $4.75, which is the price we have made available to him now.
With regard to the hon. member's question about $4.75 milk, the statement is very clear. It is very specific. I know the hon. member understands it, and I hope he does not wish to delude either this chamber or the farmers in any way. What we have said is that our support policy will enable factories to pay $3.54 for milk which, with the $1.21 subsidy, will give a price of $4.75 for milk.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
As I said last year and repeat now, we have no authority to force factories to pay any price whatsoever. We have a support program that will enable them to pay $3.54. In the province of Ontario machinery has been set up which will compel the factories to pay this price when the support program enables them to do so. The minister in the province of Quebec has assured me that in the ensuing year they will have similar machinery available so that they will be in a position to fix the price. In the province of Quebec and possibly in other parts of Canada there are remote areas in which there are casein and roller powder plants which may not be able to pay this price. This applies particularly in respect of casein. The minister in the province of Quebec has assured me that as a result of the savings which will ensue from our taking over the support in respect of manufacturing milk they will be able to supplement provincially those areas in which the companies cannot pay the $3.54.
I should like to make it abundantly clear that I have never said that we are fixing the price, that we can fix the price, or have the authority to do so. The statistics I have indicate that in some areas, particularly in Quebec, some factories may not be able to pay this price but, from the statements which have been made to me, the provincial government will put them in a position to pay it then in fact the factory will pay this price to the producer.

Mr. Chairman, I am stressing this problem because it is extremely important. We were told, last year, that our dairy policy would give the farmers, the producers of industrial milk, an average of $4 per hundredweight of milk and it is precisely this $4 per hundredweight that allowed certain industries to avoid paying that price.
Now, since the minister tells us that his government is granting the necessary aid to

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
enable industry to pay $3.54 per hundredweight could he say whether the assistance his department is giving the dairy industry is designed to secure a minimum of $3.54 per hundredweight?
Does he not feel it would be better to set a minimum price the manufacturers or the processors would have to pay the milk producers, as he has said that his department was giving all the necessary assistance and the required support so that the milk industry could be in a position to pay $3.54 per hundredweight of milk?
Since the federal government is providing the assistance necessary for a minimum payment of $3.54, why is his Department not setting a minimum price of $3.54 per hundredweight as the price to be paid by the operators of the milk industry to the milk producers?

Mr. Chairman, as I explained before, the best advice I have is that at the federal level we do not have the authority to fix prices within a province. This is a provincial responsibility. I do not know whether it will be feasible in all the provinces to have boards which set prices. Certainly, however, this is a matter which will be discussed by me with the provincial ministers. I know this already has been done in the province of Ontario and I am assured by the minister that it will be done in the province of Quebec. Surely this should answer the fears of my hon. friend concerning the $3.54 being paid, provided that the action which I have been assured will be taken is carried out by the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, it is an important problem. I realize that everyone is anxious to complete as soon as possible, the consideration of those estimates; nevertheless, I would have one or two questions to put to the minister.
Could the minister tell me whether his Department would object to the payment of additional subsidies by the Quebec government, if the dairy industry was unable to pay the price of $3.54 per hundredweight of industrial milk?

Mr. Chairman, the problems in respect of provincial subsidies which arose last year made life very difficult for those provinces which did not have the subsidies.

When a subsidy in one province enables a manufacturer in that province to produce more cheaply than a manufacturer in another province, this leads to an unnatural flow of the product across the provinces and makes it difficult for the federal government to exercise its responsibility equitably over the movement of the product across provincial boundaries. Accordingly, the ministers from the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario and I met and resolved the problem as best we could. I believe we reached a viable solution. It was agreed that provincial subsidies would be removed provided that the federal program for the ensuing year included an increase of a minimum of 25 cents. This has been done. It was made quite clear, however, that in areas such as those which have casein or roller powder plants, or other remote areas where the plants are not able to pay the $3.54, the province of Quebec would have every right to subsidize those producers up to the $3.54 level.
It was suggested that the funds they would save by reason of the Federal increase in our support level, which I understand would amount to $8 million or $9 million, could be used for that purpose and, along with capital expenditures, for the purpose of rationalization of the industries in those areas which do not have economic plants or, in particular, in which there is a desire to carry out a conversion from casein.

Mr. Chairman, if I understand correctly the minister's statement, his department would see no objection in allowing the Quebec government to pay additional subsidies which would enable the leaders of the dairy industry to pay $3.54 for a hundredweight of milk?
In my view, that is what his statement is all about.

I think that is quite correct. I might add that I would be somewhat presumptuous if I were to tell any province what kind of subsidies it should provide. I think it was agreed that if there were to be provincial subsidies they should be equalized, that is, that a disparity in respect of subsidies between one province and another would not lead to an efficient and economic industry. In our deliberations, however, I believe the provincial ministers preferred to get out of the business of subsidies on manufacturing milk in consideration of a better federal program

and in turn we believe the responsibility in respect of fluid milk should remain with the provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I have another question for the Minister of Agriculture-

Mr. Chairman, I should not like to let this opportunity pass without assuring the minister that I do not belong to the school which believes in the weights and measures criterion. I belong to the school which believes we should get away from this spending spree but not at the expense of the farmers. The 33 J per cent figure in which the minister took such pride is relative to the amount of milk produced and does not relate to dollars and cents. We should look at production and methods of providing farmers with a better way of living.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend te take part in this discussion at this time but I cannot let the minister's partisan remarks go by without comment. He suggested that the facts put on record by those of my colleagues who are not present at this time in the house were substantially incorrect. Will the minister accept the facts in respect of agriculture put forward by my colleagues or does he stand by his figures and say that the farmers in Canada never had it so good?

Mr. Chairman, those are the hon. member's words, not mine. My remarks and the statistics I placed on the record clearly indicate that from the standpoint of productivity the Canadian farmer is doing the best job he has ever done and the best job being done by farmers in any part of the world. From the standpoint of gross income we have made considerable improvement. I have said time and time again, and if this is what the hon. gentleman has reference to I agree with him, that we have done quite a bit but must do a great deal more. On the other hand, we cannot contribute to the accomplishment of better policies or a better way of life for the farmer by mis-stating the facts or misleading the farmers by suggesting that farming is a dying industry and there is no

March 22, 1967
Supply-Agriculture
hope. That attitude will not contribute anything. I take exception to this attitude when expressed by hon. members. My contention is that we have done a great deal but we must do more.

A further question, Mr. Chairman.
The Minister of Agriculture knows that when a dairy producer produces fluid milk for bottling, the dairy fixes a quota, and when such a quota is exceeded for an additional quantity of 20 per cent, the dairy no longer has to pay a minimum or average price to dairy producers. Therefore, this means that if a farmer has a 500-pound quota and he comes to the dairy with 700 pounds of milk, he will get his maximum or the average price on 500 pounds, but on the extra 200 pounds he may as well get $2.00, $2.25 or $2.30 per hundredweight. In this way, his average price for 700 pounds of milk is greatly reduced.
Can the minister tell us whether, under the new dairy policy announced today, dairies will have to pay $3.54 per hundredweight for any surplus, above the quota fixed, that will be used as bottled fluid milk, but as manufacturing milk to be processed into butter, cheese and other dairy products? In other words, will the policy announced today also apply to any surplus, starting with the first pound of milk, above the quotas fixed by the dairies?

Mr. Chairman, the statement very clearly indicates that responsibility for the fluid milk industry as far as we are concerned now rests with the provinces. No matter how hard everyone tries to do his best it is difficult to devise effective programs when there is mixed jurisdictions. As a result of our agreement with the provinces last year, under which we accept responsibility for the support of manufacturing milk, we deemed it in the interest of the industry generally that we should leave the entire authority and jurisdiction in respect of fluid milk with the provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I am not referring to the quantity of fluid milk for bottling sold by the dairy farmer, I am talking about that part of the small producer's milk to be used as manufactured milk and processed by the manufacturer. I am dealing only with that part used as manufactured

milk and brought by the farmer to the dairy in excess of the quota fixed by the dairy.
I shall therefore repeat my question. If a farmer brings 700 lbs. of milk to the dairy when his quota is fixed at 500 lbs., that quantity will be bottled and sold as fluid milk. Then, that quantity of milk will come under provincial jurisdiction, but will the remaining 200 lbs. used as manufactured milk and processed as butter, cheese or other products be subject to the new dairy policy announced today by the minister? That is what I want to know.
