speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a question I should like to put to the minister under this item which calls for an additional grant of $800,000 to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am not against the grant but I have a question I should like to ask; indeed, I have a suggestion to make.
On January 16 this year I filed a question on the order paper in which I asked for figures covering the calendar year 1966. My question asked how much money had been spent by the various departments of the government on advertising over C.B.C. radio, C.B.C. television, private radio and private television.
My question was made an order for return on March 13, 1967, and a return was tabled that day which is identified as sessional paper No. 238C. I must say that I was a bit amazed to discover from the information contained in

March 22, 1967
Supply-C.B.C.
this return that with the exception of one department of the federal government all the departments that do any advertising over radio or television stations spend considerably more money on the private radio and television stations than they do in advertising over the C.B.C. The minister will see immediately why I indicated that I had a suggestion to make to him, that if the C.B.C. needs some extra money maybe one of the ways we could do it would be by transferring government advertising from private stations to the public stations, or at least by doing it on something of a 50-50 basis-not the one horse, one rabbit, a suggestion that was made earlier today.
I will not take the time of the committee to put all the figures on the record; as I say, they are contained in sessional paper No. 238C. But let me give the totals. The total amount spent by the government in advertising over C.B.C. radio last year was $67,511, and over C.B.C. television stations $149,733. I am omitting the cents. But the government spent in advertising over private radio stations $510,246, and over private television stations $502,711. If I may go one step further and just add those figures together, both radio and television, it adds up to an expenditure of $217,255 in advertising over the C.B.C. but $1,012,958 in advertising over private radio and television stations. There is a difference there of almost 5 to 1. In fact, in one of the minister's own departments-I am thinking of the minister as having three departments, the Treasury Board, taxation and customs -Treasury Board and customs apparently did no advertising of this kind, whereas the taxation people spent $3,857 in advertising over C.B.C. but $77,854 in advertising over private radio.
I am going to ask the minister for an explanation. I ask why this kind of advertising is not divided a little more evenly between the two broadcasting regimes in this country; and does he not agree that here is a way where money might be obtained by the C.B.C. for advertising services rendered, rather than having to make a grant at this time? I do not wish it to be inferred that I think the advertising that is done is all worth while. Some of it is, but I think some of it is not. I am not going into that matter now; I am going, rather, into the question of the inequity of the way in which this advertising money is spent.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, of course I cannot speak for all advertising that is done and how it is divided as between C.B.C. radio and private radio stations. But I can speak with

respect to my particular department and the taxation division. The advertising that is carried out on radio is allocated in order to achieve coverage in all cities in Canada and all areas of Canada.
There is a much greater number of private radio stations than C.B.C. stations. The C.B.C. stations cover the major markets. Where these stations exist, they are used. Every station is covered by the advertising agency based on listener reports. They are selected by the agency in order to obtain maximum coverage. There was no television involved with regard to my department. To obtain the coverage we wanted in the areas we wished to cover, we had to use far more private stations in number, and consequently in dollars, than C.B.C. stations.

speechtext: I would still like to suggest to the minister, in his capacity as President of the Treasury Board, which looks at these expenditures, that he take another look at this question of the government spending five times as much on private stations as on the C.B.C.

Mr. Chairman, since parliament has given us practically no opportunity to discuss matters relating to the C.B.C.-the latest example of that was when the estimates of the C.B.C. were withdrawn from the committee on broadcasting and brought into the full house a few weeks ago-I should like to make some comments on this vote. Since the C.B.C. gives no information to anybody, they cannot be said to have a spokesman in the house. I have referred to the Secretary of State on several occasions as representing the C.B.C. She certainly does not answer for it, as she is never given any information with which to answer questions.
March 22, 1967

I can say that I can state the position of the C.B.C. with regard to the most recent exchange between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the Minister of National Revenue. One reason for the great disparity in the moneys paid out to private stations as compared to those paid the C.B.C. is that private stations have a much greater audience appeal and a much larger number of listeners and viewers. This can be proved by the Bureau of Broadcast Measurement. If the cabinet wishes to reach the largest number of viewers and listeners for the money it is spending, it has to use private stations.
It will be interesting to have an analysis made of the figures which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just produced to see how much money was spent on private stations which are located in centres where there is also a C.B.C. station. I find it hard to believe, after having been in the advertising business for 40 years, that the disparity could not be reduced in the smaller communities where the C.B.C. does not have an outlet, especially in view of the fact that rates are not very high in these smaller communities. The most interesting comparison would be between the money that is spent on private stations in centres where there is a C.B.C. outlet and places where they operate alone. I do not expect this information will be given to us much before one or one and a half years have elapsed, at which time we will have forgotten about the whole matter.
My purpose in rising now is to ask two questions. I note that in the past few days that great Canadian commentator, Mr. James F. Minifie, who is a full fledged American citizen and therefore is in a position to look through Canadian eyes at affairs going on in Washington and in the United States, and is able to tell us stay-at-home Canadians how he looks at Canadian affairs, has recently made a trip to Guam with the President of the United States. If it is at all possible I should like to ascertain whether or not the C.B.C. paid anything for the passage of Mr. Minifie, a United States citizen, because of the attack made by Mr. Knowlton Nash on three Canadian newspapermen alleging that when they took part in an aeroplane trip to South Viet Nam paid for by the United States government their opinions were therefore coloured. If these newspapermen's opinions were coloured by the fact that they flew to South Viet Nam at no expense, what about the opinions of Mr. Minifie who flew to Guam? If we are told that
Supply-C.B.C.
Mr. Minifie's expenses were paid, can we ascertain from the C.B.C. how much the C.B.C. paid for that trip?
If he was only paid $100 or so, as a token
payment, which is nothing compared to what it would cost to fly from Washington to Guam, survey the scene and fly back, then there is nothing more to say. Otherwise I do not see how the C.B.C. can allow a man like Mr. Nash to stand before the microphones and accuse people who fly to South Viet Nam at the expense of the United States government of being biased in their opinions, while a fellow citizen commentator, Mr. Minifie, flies to Guam and back and we have to believe that his opinions are absolutely crystal clear and pure. If the C.B.C. would stop attacking competing media and look after its own house, it would be much better. I would ask the minister to ascertain how much money the C.B.C. paid for Mr. Minifie's flight to Guam.
Has the C.B.C. taken a definite stand to do everything possible to offend the U.S. government? I have stood in this house on numerous occasions and stated that, come what may, the foreign policy of this nation should be to maintain the closest possible friendship with the United States. I will repeat this tonight. In the last 24 hours we were told about a group of U.S. citizens who, according to the United States government, were violating the United States law in taking medical supplies to North Viet Nam by launch from Hong Kong. They are going to North Viet Nam with $10,000 worth of medical supplies. I say: All power to them, and God bless them in the work of compassion which they are performing. I certainly do not criticize them.
We are told, when we are performing any works of compassion, not to let our left hand know what our right hand is doing. I do not know of any organization that is getting more free publicity for their limited work in helping the injured in North Viet Nam than the organization which is operating that launch from Hong Kong to Hanoi. Yet why is the C.B.C. sending a man to travel alongside the launch in preparation of an hour long documentary? Is the C.B.C. going to spend its time to show that the United States government is performing great outrages in North Viet Nam and at the same time prepare a documentary on these fine gentlemen who are going out in a launch with medical supplies, to show the fine work they are doing?
The $10,000 in gifts going to North Viet Nam is nothing compared to the value of the free advertising that this trip in a launch is

March 22, 1967
Supply-C.B.C.
receiving. Why does the C.B.C. have to commission a freelancer to go along and make a documentary of the trip? Is it not enough to tell us that medical supplies are being run to North Viet Nam and the United States does not like it? Why does the C.B.C., which is paid for from Canadian government funds, have to have a man following the launch to prepare a documentary showing that $10,000 worth of medical supplies are being brought to North Viet Nam? It is galling, the way the C.B.C. is eternally needling the United States and its attitude with regard to North Viet Nam, as well as its attitude in other parts of the world where the United States government has to take an active stand while more supine governments take no stand at all. Why is the C.B.C. always needling the United States?
Can the minister ascertain whether the C.B.C. is paying for Mr. Minifie's trip to Guam and back, and can he also advise us whether the C.B.C. has taken a definite anti-U.S. stand in the light of the fact that Beryl Fox had been sent to South Viet Nam, and now this freelancer is going to North Viet Nam?
I should like to ask the hon. gentleman who just spoke whether he knows it as a fact that Knowlton Nash is a United States citizen?
I never made such a statement. I said Mr. Minifie is a United States citizen. I do not have enough interest in Knowlton Nash to inquire what his citizenship is.

Mr. Chairman, I was only going to take about five minutes of the time of the committee to make my comments, and I would not even take up that much time except for what the previous speaker has mentioned, namely that we never get a chance to discuss the C.B.C. in this house. In fact we have not had such a chance for years, except for the briefest exchanges during the question period.
There are one or two points which I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. I do not suppose that my comments will make any difference in the outcome because this extra expenditure will be approved this time. I should like to know who if anybody in the C.B.C.-and I suspect no one-has any control over the amount of money that is spent on these trips, and what is their purpose.
People are being sent on such junkets as this trip to North Viet Nam to cover the Quaker launch taking supplies to Hanoi, and

we could name many more instances. I realize that people in the C.B.C. think there is a limitless well of money, and all they have to do is ask for it, that no matter what the purpose of such an expenditure might be, parliament will grant it. To be fair, I do not blame the C.B.C. officials for thinking this because the supine parliament, of which I have been a member for many years has always voted, almost without question, whatever amount of money the C.B.C. has asked for. As I said earlier, parliament seldom gets the opportunity to do much questioning of the operations of the C.B.C.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
As the previous speaker very well pointed out, the C.B.C. seems to be more interested in being anti-American than it is in looking after the problems in Canada. They send all sorts of people down to the southern United States to take pictures, make documentaries and all the rest about the very difficult race problems existing in the southern United States. This is of some interest to Canadians, of course; but for a while every time you turned on the radio or a television set all you would hear about was the problems of the southern United States.
The C.B.C. should spend more of the taxpayers' money on trying to better the lot of the Canadian Indians and Eskimos and some of the other groups in this country. This would be much better than spending much of their time broadcasting the problems of other countries. Though these may be of some interest to Canadians, they are not of paramount interest. Our main interest is, or should be, the problems we in Canada face, and we should be told how we can cure them. I suspect that some of the people in the C.B.C.-for what reason I know not, though I have my suspicions-want to do all they can to damage the image and reputation of the United States in Canada; and we all know who will benefit the most from this.
There are many other examples I could cite in this regard, Mr. Chairman, but my time is limited. I should like whoever is replying for the C.B.C. just to cite one example during the course of the last two or three years, or even further back than that, of a program that was even neutral in content toward the United States. All of the programs I have heard were violently anti-American, and I am a constant listener to the C.B.C. We will have a great deal more to say on this matter on another occasion, but I think this matter should be brought before the house as often as possible.
March 22, 1967	COMMONS
One of the main criticisms I have heard of the C.B.C.-and it is one of my own as well-is that some people in the C.B.C. seem to have a God-given mission, a self-appointed one, I may add, to know what is best for the people of Canada and they make sure that Canadians get it whether they like it or not. They decide a certain economic policy or political policy or social policy is good for Canadians and they ram it down our throats. All you have to do is listen to any of the commentators on programs, or C.B.C. spokesmen, and you will see what I mean.
I have no objection to some people in the C.B.C. wishing to make it a policy to brainwash the public, provided both sides of a controversial subject are presented. I know that there is, of course, a very practical disadvantage to this suggestion, because if the brain trusters in the C.B.C. decide to promote anti-Americanism, or socialism, or something else, they will do so. Then if they are asked to present the other side of the picture, all they will do is to put on the program people who do not present a very good case for the other side. That is all they will do and I know that perfectly well.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, I think that some sort of body should be given the power to make regulations. Certainly the Board of Broadcast Governors do not do their job, that's for sure; otherwise we would not have this problem. I suppose a lot of people like to be appointed to the board because it gives them some prestige and they never do anything. I think they should pay more attention to their jobs.
To return to the subject, before the C.B.C. is given a lot more money by this parliament it should be impressed upon that organization that they will not get it unless controversial subjects of great public interest are presented in a fashion which shows both points of view. This has never been done to date, and I think it should.
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, because we all wish to get things completed as soon as possible; but I know that a good many of my colleagues on both sides of the house will have more to say on this subject.

In order to save time I want briefly to quote from the Globe and Mail for January 14, 1967, which contained this article by Mr. Bruce Macdonald from Washington:
Largely as a result of water storage facilities provided by Canada under the Columbia River treaty, the power-generating capacity of Grand Coulee dam in Washington state will be increased from the present level of almost two million kilowatts to a proposed output in the 1990's of 9.2 million kilowatts, making the Grand Coulee the largest power dam in the world.
Interior Secretary Stewart Udall announced yesterday that a start had been authorized on the addition at once of a further 3.6 million kilowatts, as anticipated at the time the agreement was signed with Canada for the joint development of the Columbia River power and flood-control facilities.
Further on in the article the following appears:
Despite the U.S. contention, Canadian sources-
We do not know at the moment who they were.
-expected that officials in Ottawa would almost certainly scrutinize the complex formula laid down in the treaty with Washington to determine whether the addition of power-generating capacity would entitle Canada to claim increased compensation.
Canadian officials noted that even if the total power output was no greater than anticipated at the time the treaty was signed, it was possible the fine print would show that British Columbia was entitled to a higher payment if the extra power produced was used to meet peak demand and was therefore capable of being sold to power distributors at a higher price than electricity for base demands.
Then under the subheading "Canada sold down river, Toronto economist says", Mr. Macdonald writes:
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)

Also I want to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in these supplementary estimates there will be found eight times the expression "notwithstanding" some act already on the statute books of the nation. This means that these supplementary estimates, if passed in their present form, will set aside the requirements of eight pieces of legislation. For instance, under vote 6g of the Department of External Affairs we are asked to set aside section 35 of the Financial Administration Act. This is money that has been received from the people. It has been taken in by the Receiver General of Canada and paid into the consolidated revenue fund. Why cannot this money be taken by the Receiver General of Canada into the consolidated revenue fund in the same way as all other moneys are received? I do not see any urgency about setting up tonight a separate organization to accept this money from a foreign government. It will not be embarrassed by any delay caused by the time taken to bring in a bill to create the change suggested in this one-dollar item.

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion every Canadian has the right to adequate shelter. We have been told that we need 170,000 housing starts per year just to keep up with the present level of accommodation. Last year we had only 134,000 starts. Why? I submit there are three or four basic causes.
The first cause is high labour costs. More important is the federal government's sales tax, municipal taxes and a tight money policy. We in this party have been pressing for the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax which is applied at the manufacturers level. We have been pressing for its removal with good and just reason, because we find that this tax, innocuous as it appears to be at 11 per cent, by the time it hits the ultimate consumer has been marked up by the various levels through which it passes until it reaches 15 per cent or 16 per cent.
I have been a member of the consumer credit committee, which has been informed that in the average home costing $15,000 to $18,000 roughly 60 per cent of the cost is accounted for by material, and by the time the various profits are made on the sales tax at the various levels, instead of this tax amounting to $1,000 on such a house, as it normally would, it winds up being between $1,500 to $1,600.
We definitely have a housing crisis. In fact reference has been made to a fiasco in the housing industry. I submit that the cost of government at various levels, municipal, provincial and federal is to blame to some degree.
March 22, 1967

I was recently interested to read a statement by Mr. Hignett, President of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to the effect that the average self-contained three bedroom home probably has a municipal tax burden of $38 to $40 per month, due to services which the public demands, and which has resulted in the fact that the average person earning $5,000 to $6,000 per year can no longer own or even attempt to own a home.
Another situation is developing whereby people living in limited dividend housing and subsidized housing are being forced out of such homes due to the actions of the government. Indeed at Saint John, New Brunswick, there are at present 30 or 40 vacancies in public housing because the formula which is used for rental accommodation is based on the gross take home pay of the renters. Due to the money which the government takes from the average wage earners' pay packet in Canada Pension Plan contributions, hospital insurance, income tax and all the other deductions, he can no longer afford to stay in subsidized socialized housing. Therefore the 25 per cent to 27 per cent figure which is applied to total income in establishing rental for such a person must be re-examined. In other words the percentage figure must be applied to what such poor people have left over after the government has dipped into their pay packets first. We have welfare stated ourselves so far that such people cannot afford subsidized socialized housing.
Due to lack of action by the government, and lack of an adequate housing plan, the government has spread the mantle of poverty over those in the low income bracket until it now reaches up into the class I choose to call the affluent poor, those in the $5,000 to $6,000 per year category, who should be able to own houses but who cannot.
I shall not take up the time of the committee further, Mr. Chairman. I just close with one statement with which I think no one will disagree, namely that housing should not be the victim of government tight money policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Chaimran, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent has introduced a very important issue, that of housing. On Monday afternoon my colleague, the hon. member for Danforth, attempted to initiate an emergency debate on the housing crisis. He pointed out that the government has had a housing policy fiasco and that it has reached the point of being a critical national calamity and national disgrace. He also pointed out that the Minister of Labour, in charge of housing, in the
Supply-Labour
midst of this crisis remains serene, indifferent and unconcerned. That was on Monday of this week.
In today's Ottawa Citizen there appears an article quoting statements made by the Minister of Labour on the housing crisis. I read it in part as follows:
Canada is coming out of its house-building crisis. Labour Minister J. R. Nicholson contended Tuesday.
But the new houses are going to cost too much for the average Canadian to own if they're located in major cities, he readily admitted-
"Housing problems are going to be serious for an indefinite period," he concluded. "But I would hope that the crisis period is over."
Mr. Nicholson offered no hope that the cost of housing would decline as new housing becomes available.
He said high land values would continue to prevent Canadians from getting the housing they wanted in major cities.
"If you're going to live in a city you're going to have to live in an apartment," he said.
The alternative was to move to the suburbs, he explained. Or if you wanted to own your own apartment you could resort to condominium housing which had just been approved in British Columbia and Alberta.
That is the approach being taken by the minister to the housing crisis. In 1965 there were 165,000 new homes built in Canada. In 1966 the figure was 134,000, a drop of 19 per cent. The projected housing goal for 1967 is 170,000 units, set by the Economic Council of Canada and confirmed by the President of C.M.H.C. But in the first two months of this year there has been a serious drop in housing starts, so serious that it prompted the hon. member for Danforth to bring it to the attention of the house.
An article in the Globe and Mail of March 8 stated:
It is not news that Canada is moving into a housing crisis. Last fall the Economic Council of Canada warned that anything short of 170,000 housing starts a year would result in a serious shortage-[DOT]
Central Mortgage this week confirmed everybody's worst expectations. Total urban housing starts in January, it reported, nosedived 29.6 per cent compared with last January. Toronto's starts were down by an alarming 59.2 per cent, and Toronto and Montreal, which also showed a decline, are the housing weathervanes of the country-
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
Yet no spirit of haste is evident in either national or provincial government. Federal Labour Minister J. R. Nicholson has announced that loans for 20,000 new housing units will be distributed in the spring -a mere drop in the bucket; that funds available under the National Housing Act will be increased from $600 million to $800 million; and that he is contemplating some changes in the act. Ontario

March 22, 1987
Supply-Labour
has promised to launch its dubious Home Ownership Made Easy program, for buying up land and leasing it at nominal sums to would-be home owners.
This is the approach the minister is taking. He says there will be 20,000 new units in the spring and that the reason for the drop in January and February this year is that the direct loans last year were made in the summer. He says that this year they will be made in the spring and the result will be a projected increase in housing starts.
Another approach was to increase the interest rates on N.H.A. mortgages from 7| per cent to 7J per cent. He also hopes there will be an increase in housing because of the participation of the banks in the mortgage lending field. This is the approach the minister takes to our housing crisis. In the past few months he has held a housing symposium in many cities across the country. He has heard from the builders about the serious lack of mortgage money. He has heard from the developers about the serious lack of serviced land, and he has heard from other representatives about the serious rise in the cost of homes. I recall that Mr. Mansur, who has been called Mr. Housing in Canada, indicated that Canadians have outpriced themselves in the cost of homes. He said that mortgage money is available but that the costs are so prohibitive that purchasers of homes are not being attracted. In Toronto the average cost of a home is $29,000. In order to carry that type of home one would have to have an income of between $8,000 and $10,000. This would indicate that any person with an income below that amount would be left homeless, in the full sense of the word, when one thinks of adequate housing.
It might be said that it is very easy to be critical and that it is better to become constructive with regard to a definite housing program. We in the New Democratic Party have attempted to be constructive. We have impressed upon the minister the need for a ministry of housing and urban development. By this means we would be in a position to provide leadership to the country in respect of housing needs and to encourage the provinces and the municipalities to participate in a massive housing program to fulfil the needs of the low income groups, middle income groups, senior citizens, and those people who wish to participate in co-operative housing projects. We believe the government should inject a massive amount of money into the economy for mortgage loans at interest rates

of 5 per cent or 6 per cent. These would be reasonable rates at which people could afford to buy homes. Someone may ask, where will we get this money. The amount has been increased from $600 million to $800 million. We have suggested, and I suggest again tonight, that we should participate in home bonds. We believe the government should float bonds at attractive rates of interest in the same way they did during wartime when they promoted the victory bonds to prosecute the war.
We should float home bonds so that Canadians would be in a position to participate in a program which would ensure that there would be decent housing for all Canadians. The government should also take the initiative in respect of public housing. The government has not been able to persuade the provincial and municipal governments to participate sufficiently in public housing in order to take care of the needs of the people who have incomes ranging between $4,000 and $6,000. The result is that there is a tremendous shortage of apartments for these people. The apartments which are available are available at very high rentals.
During the housing symposium a suggestion was made that the government should take a more active interest in limited dividend housing. At the moment the government guarantees a return of 5 per cent on limited dividend housing. The suggestion was made that there would be more participation by builders if the guaranteed return on their investment was between 8 per cent and 9 per cent. We are in agreement with this suggestion. Because of the serious housing shortage some inducement must be given to builders and developers.
One of the saddest commentaries we have in centennial year is the serious plight in which our senior citizens find themselves today. Our senior citizens who are on fixed incomes are paying very high rent for apartments and rooms. Because of the high cost of living this represents a very great drain on their limited assets and income. This is the reason the government really should encourage the provinces and municipalities to build more homes for the senior citizens so that their needs can be fulfilled. Co-operative housing also should be encouraged so that those people who have the desire to build their homes could be given help, so that they would be in a position to finance their homes.
The hon. member for Lambton-Kent mentioned a very important problem with regard
March 22, 1967

to the cost of homes today. One reason is the 12 per cent sales tax that is imposed on building materials, and the 5 per cent provincial tax. Both these items should be eliminated in respect of residential homes in particular, if these homes are to be sold at prices which will be attractive to purchasers.
These are a few ideas which we would hope the Minister of Labour would consider seriously, rather than continue in the belief he has now that there is a constitutional barrier with regard to full participation in this important matter. He seems to believe that his only role at the moment is that of the friendly banker. We disagree with this and hope that he will forge ahead and give the necessary leadership to meet the housing crisis, so that Canadians in 1967 will have a housing program of which they can be proud.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize it is getting late, but some of us believe that we should not go away from the house at this time without again drawing the attention of the government to the magnitude of the housing crisis, and the fact that all of us have had our attention drawn to the plight of the people all across the country who are suffering because of the lack of decisive action in dealing with the problem at this time.
My colleague from Toronto-Broadview has pointed out the way in which the minister is indulging in optimistic and hopeful predictions about what will happen in respect of housing this year. Actually the members of his staff are much less optimistic than the minister.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I wish the minister were here tonight but I have no doubt his duties require him to be elsewhere. I should like to urge him to take his head out of the sand and look around to see what is happening in respect of housing today. His head is far too decorative a part of his anatomy to be left in the sand. He should look around to see what is happening, rather than hide behind the rosy vision which he obviously has in respect of what he hopes housing starts are likely to be. He should realize that something more far-reaching has to be done in respect of this very difficult housing situation. It is time the minister stopped predicting housing starts and began to do something to help provide the 170,000 new homes we will need for this current year. That number of new houses will not be of any assistance in reducing the backlog that has been built up.
Supply-Labour
The committee on prices heard a great deal of evidence across Canada about the need to deal with the housing shortage in a much more comprehensive manner. I wish to make a few remarks about the situation in my city of Vancouver because I have had a great number of representations from people who live there, and because I feel that that city is fairly representative of larger Canadian cities. Those things which are evident in Vancouver are evident in most of the major cities in Canada.
On February 1 the director of planning for the Vancouver city council prepared a series of notes for the use of aldermen at the housing conference. I do not believe those notes were used to any extent during that conference but I should like to quote one paragraph. The director of planning wrote the following:
Much has been written about housing needs in Vancouver and elsewhere, yet no major Canadian city appears to have made a comprehensive survey of such needs. The city of Vancouver in 1960 and 1961 budgeted for its share of a $36,000 metropolitan housing survey to be financed 75 per cent by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under Part V of the National Housing Act, and 25 per cent by lower mainland municipalities. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, however, declined to participate.
In 1960-61 the city of Vancouver realized the need for a comprehensive survey of housing needs in the city at that time, and that was six or seven years ago. At that time the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had the rosy idea that if things were left to the workings of the market sufficient housing would be provided in the city of Vancouver. Vancouver is still waiting for the C.M.H.C. to approve this plan. However, the city is now trying to get another survey under way, which has been approved by the council, endorsed by the province and referred to the corporation. It will cost in the neighbourhood of $96,000. That approval has not been forthcoming.
It is my belief that such a survey is crucial in every large city from Vancouver to Halifax because we do not know how many housing starts are necessary. Very little consideration has been given as to the kinds of housing needed or the number of each kind. I think if the policy of C.M.H.C. and the minister continues we will spend an increasing number of the taxpayers' dollars to assist the better off people in our community. The people of moderate and low incomes will not get any help, or not as much as they should get. We will then have a situation in which socialism will provide for the rich, and free enterprise will

March 22, 1967
Supply-Labour
provide for the poor. The rich have decided that socialism is necessary in order that they may obtain C.M.H.C. loans and that the poor should be left to the tender mercies of free enterprise.
The president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation appeared before our committee on January 26 of this year and stated:
Nevertheless, Canada's housing policies in the past have been based on the assumption that the determination of a very large part of our housing production can be left to market forces.
He then went on to say that a very large and increasing proportion of our housing needs cannot be met by private enterprise alone. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent pointed out that we were told by individuals appearing before the committee that people with incomes under $6,000 per annum could not afford to own homes. I am sure that even the minister is beginning to realize, with reluctance, that even though a great number of homes will be built the people who need live in them will not be able to own them.
The Vancouver Housing Association prepared a brief for our committee in which it stated in respect of home ownership:
So far as home ownership is concerned, building costs, after remaining fairly static in the Vancouver area for several years, rose by 7 per cent between the springs of 1965 and 1966, and have since risen further. Prices of serviced residential lots have risen during the last five years by anything from 10 per cent to 100 per cent according to location, with an average increase of perhaps 25 per cent, and today it is difficult to buy serviced lots in suburban municipalities for much less than $5,000.
High mortgage interest rates aggravate the effects of rising building and land costs and, while no specific figures are available to us, there are indications that a good many families are tying up an excessive proportion of their income in housing outlays.
This statement is confirmed by what Michael Wheeler of the Canadian Welfare Council wrote in a submission to our committee. He said:
We have no reliable data on the number of families who are enjoying the pleasures of home ownership at the cost of severely strained budgets, nor do we know the actual cost of this strain in terms of other budgetary items that have to be sacrificed or its general impact on family well-being. This is a matter which, like so many other aspects of Canada's housing program, deserves more systematic attention.
I am urging that there should be more planning and an overall survey made in respect of housing needs. In respect of home ownership even the minister is now convinced that we are not going to meet the needs of a

great many people in lower and middle income groups.
This is what was said by the Vancouver housing association in its brief to our committee:
A canvass of leading real estate firm suggests that apartments falling vacant are renting for amounts from 5 per cent to 10 per cent higher than six months earlier, but in the low rental field increases have been much steeper. Within the last month elderly single persons applying for non-profit housing at the Central Housing registry operated by our association have reported the following increases in their rents:-
From $45 to $75 (excluding heat)
$45 to $80
$45 to $85 (shared bathroom)
Vacancies in rental housing, where families with children are accepted, are, according to real estate firms, virtually non-existent, so that it is difficult to quote any meaningful figures, but rents often appear now to be related more closely to what the traffic will bear than to the actual worth of the accommodation.
The greatest single need of Vancouver is low rental accommodation for middle and low income families. As a matter of fact, the director of the war on poverty made the statement as long ago as last fall to the Cou-chiching conference that Canada is spending more money on tinned dog food than it is on public housing. That certainly does not say very much for our degree of civilization.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
There is a tremendous need in Canada for housing for low and moderate income families. If hon. members need an example to underline this I would refer to the matter raised a while ago in this house when it was pointed out that the immigration officials in Europe are saying to would-be immigrants to Canada, "Yes, come to Canada by all means. But if you do come, and have more than three children, do not go to any major Canadian city." They named half a dozen, including Vancouver. They said, Do not go to any major Canadian city unless you have a guaranteed income of at least $7,500 a year.
This reminds me of the old nursery rhyme. I am emboldened to quote poetry after what happened last night:
"Mother, may I go down to swim?"
"Yes, my darling daughter.
Hang your clothes on a hickory limb;
But don't go near-
-Vancouver, Halifax, Toronto, Montreal or many of the major cities in between, because you will not find housing there." That is the situation in this country. We have only to consider places like Birmingham and others
March 22, 19S7

in Britain, to which people immigrated and where there was no adequate housing, to see what happens to the good feeling and good neighbourliness at all levels vis-a-vis people already living in those areas.
This further question concerns Central Mortgage and Housing. Family formation is going ahead by leaps and bounds these days. Not only are new families rapidly being formed but we are finding greater and greater mobility in Canada. Many young couples would not want to own homes even if they could afford them. They must have rental accommodation, because we are told that one family in four across Canada moves every year. We must have rental accommodation to take care of this situation.
Before I conclude my remarks I want to make a special plea to the minister and draw a special matter to his attention. In Vancouver's west end we are at long last apparently going to have a high-rise apartment block for elderly citizens. I do not know whether it will be available to the most needy among the elderly citizens. I hope it will be. But I believe a mistake, and a bad one, will be made in connection with this housing project unless something is done to prevent it.
In respect of any housing project for the elderly, of the type being built in Vancouver's west end, there should be not only self-contained apartments with kitchens but a main dining room with a kitchen attached, and there should be provision whereby elderly people can have meals taken up to their rooms in case of need. The last advice I received from Central Mortgage and Housing was that it does not propose to put these facilities in the new, high-rise apartment block being built in the west end of Vancouver. I would urge the minister to change his mind in this regard and see that these facilities are provided before the project is completed.
I would remind hon. members that the social welfare and housing people urged the minister and Central Mortgage and Housing to include recreational facilities in low rent housing projects in Vancouver, for example in Skeena Terrace and other low rental, subsidized housing projects. The minister did not do this. Now, after these projects have been lived in for a number of years, and after a great deal of trouble, inconvenience and agitation, at long last Central Mortgage and Housing and the city of Vancouver are trying very hard to find ways and means of including these facilities in the Skeena Terrace
Supply-Labour
development. The facilities should have been included when the development was being built. I am warning the minister that if he does not see that these modern facilities for the care of the aged are incorporated in the new apartment block being built in Vancouver's west end, he will have to do it in a piecemeal fashion later.
There is a good more I could say on this subject, Mr. Chairman. I hope we will have a better chance to discuss housing at a later time, rather than talking about this important matter in the dying hours of interim supply. However, I will have pity on the committee because I know everyone here is just about as tired as I am. I hope the Minister of National Revenue will draw these matters to the attention of the Minister of Labour.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would simply like to say that having listened with interest to the speeches made with respect to housing, I will be most pleased to bring the matters raised by hon. members to the attention of the minister under whose jurisdiction fall the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words on his vote, as it concerns Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in particular. As hon. members are well aware, I represent a constituency which is entirely rural. The question I wish to raise concerns small towns and in some cases small contractors. I emphasize as forcibly as I can that I believe Central Mortgage and Housing has fallen back into its old rut in this respect. In 1958 and 1959, when the Conservative party formed the government, we directed C.M.H.C. to move into the smaller centres of Canada in order to help the citizens in those areas as well as those in the larger areas of this country. C.M.H.C has now fallen back into its old rut and is now concerned with helping the large contractor to build numerous homes, helter-skelter and everywhere in the larger cities. It is paying no particular attention to the smaller centres in Canada, and to our smaller contractors.
In the absence of the Minister of Labour I urge the Minister of National Revenue to bring this matter to his attention. I hope the minister will see that the small rural towns do not suffer because of the policies of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and some misguided rules and regulations that the district offices set up. I will cite a particular

March 22, 1967
Supply-Labour
case where a contractor is building a home. Before he can obtain any money from C.M.H.C. he has to have the home 85 per cent completed. I know the minister will say this cannot be true. However, it is true. This contractor is building a home for a medical doctor in a town that has a population of 3,500. The home is perhaps a little better or more extravagant than the average citizen is able to afford. In any case, Mr. Chairman, the contractor told me he would have to have the home 85 per cent completed before he could obtain one cent from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I ask the minister to urge C.M.H.C. to get out of the rut they seem to be falling into and to pay particular attention to the contractor who builds, not 200 homes a year but 20 or perhaps only 10. The minister should remember that home building conditions are not the same in small areas. It might well be said that the small contractor has higher costs because he does not build a great many homes. Of course the more homes one builds, the cheaper it is to build them. But the direct reverse is also true, because in many of our cities land costs and servicing are higher.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The servicing costs, and by that I mean wiring, sewerage, street lighting and so on, are greater in the larger areas than in the smaller towns. Therefore while I readily accept the fact that a small contractor may need a proportionately greater amount of money to build 20 houses in a year than to build 200, there is not that much difference, and I would urge the C.M.H.C. in making its inspections to make special allowances for the small contractors building in rural areas.
I could cite 100 instances of such cases all across rural Canada. The C.M.H.C. money is not being made available in the smaller areas. Time and time again small contractors have said to me. We will build a house, but please do not make us build it under C.M.H.C. because we cannot get the money, the lumber yards are after us to pay them, and we cannot get anything out of C.M.H.C. I urge the Minister of National Revenue to ask the Minister of Labour to bring this to the particular attention of C.M.H.C. to redirect its thinking toward the rural areas of Canada. Rural Canada is a vast area which needs better homes. I do not think there is one hon. member in this house who would deny that fact.

It is all well and good for us to stand up in this chamber and say that we must carry out slum clearances in our cities. But what are we actually doing? Are we making a special effort to improve the living standard of people in the rural areas and the smaller towns all across Canada? I cannot honestly say we are. The C.M.H.C. is making no special effort to improve the slum conditions which exist in the rural areas and which are just as bad as those in the cities. This is why I say to the minister it is all well and good to talk about low cost developments in the cities. We in the rural areas are not specifically asking for low cost housing. We are asking the C.M.H.C. to redirect its thinking, as has been the case in 1958, 1959 and 1961, and to give the people living in rural Canada a chance to build their houses under the C.M.H.C.
One has only to look at housing starts in rural areas under C.M.H.C. to see that what I say is correct. The first housing starts in the farm areas carried out by the C.M.H.C. were made back in 1959 and 1961. Today this has dwindled to practically nothing. We must give equal treatment to all the citizens of Canada, whether they live in cities or in rural areas.
There has been much talk about paying special attention to slum clearances and low cost housing in cities. I urge the Minister of National Revenue to ask the Minister of Labour to redirect the thinking of the C.M.H.C. so as to give the citizens in rural Canada an opportunity to build houses and to improve their standard of living, as well as to give an equal opportunity to small contractors providing services in rural areas to that given the large contractor. There is a great disparity between the two. Housing inspections in cities are much less rigid. As one contractor told me, the big contractors building houses in cities under the C.M.H.C. can get away with much more because the inspections there are much less rigid and less stringent. We in rural Canada pay taxes to improve the slum areas in cities and to build what could be qualified as subsidized housing in cities, but no special consideration is given to those living in small towns or in farming communities. It seems to me that the C.M.H.C. has taken the line of least resistance, and we in rural Canada are not satisfied with this attitude.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks on immigration before we pass it. I will take only five minutes to show how amiable I am.
This item cannot be passed over lightly because, as I said earlier this afternoon when speaking on agriculture, immigration is one of the key problems and one of Canada's key assets. We can talk about our natural resources but we must not forget that our human resource may well be our greatest. What are we doing about it? I fear that the Minister of Immigration and Manpower has come to the conclusion that only skilled immigrants or immigrants with money and capable of establishing themselves in Canada, should be admitted to our country.
I am not a member of the committee on citizenship and immigration, not because I do not wish to be but because I have not had sufficient time to devote to it. However, one has only to examine where our immigrants have settled after their arrival to Canada and where in Canada are the greatest needs for immigrants. In other words, do we need skilled or unskilled immigrants, and which of the two categories can best be absorbed? As I said this afternoon, farm labour is very scarce in Canada to day. Nine out of ten farmers anywhere in Canada are prepared to accept unskilled labour and are prepared to train these people.
We are a young country with great natural resources. Whether we like it or not we are still hewers of wood and carriers of water. It does not take too much skill to do that job. I urge the government not to restrict immigration to skilled labour, because those are not the only immigrants we need in Canada today. I have already said that we could absorb more unskilled labour. The other day I spoke to a manufacturer in Winnipeg who employs 670 men in his manufacturing plant. I asked him how he hires his men, does he hire skilled welders and machinists? Believe it or not, he said: "No, we prefer them unskilled as long as they wish to work. We are quite prepared to train them." So let us not hastily
March 22, 1987

Supply-National Defence jump on a bandwagon and think that Canada is developed and cannot absorb any more unskilled labour. Canada is a young country with much development still needed, and we still have room for immigrants who are unskilled.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
That is the key point I want to make before this particular item passes, Mr. Chairman. I recall an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal about six months ago which listed the areas in which immigrants found jobs, and nearly 45 per cent entered what could be called unskilled labour areas. I think, for example, of the servicing industry. It does not take too much skill to put gas into the tank of a car from a gas pump, an occupation which could be regarded as part of the servicing industry. They also entered agriculture and the semi-manufacturing industry, and the three industries lumped together took almost 45 per cent of the unskilled immigrants who entered Canada.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I urge the Minister of National Revenue to draw this situation to the attention of the minister of immigration. We may believe today that Canada is developed as a manufacturing country, and in the highly mechanized and technological world of today needs only skilled immigrants. This is not so. I urge the minister to continue to permit unskilled immigrants to enter Canada and to continue sponsored immigration for a few more years at least.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether this is the appropriate item for the remarks I wish to make, and if it is not perhaps I can be corrected. This afternoon there was a series of questions asked on orders of the day relating to satellite research and development in the communications field, an area in which the Department of National Defence may be interested. I know the National Research Council is working in this field, and from conversations I have had with officials in the department this field is relatively new.
A search in the library indicates that Canada has not done too much work in this field and is presently not in a position and might never be in a position to do so, for the simple reason that communications satellites cannot be sent aloft without the necessary vehicle to put them into orbit and thus make service available to areas presently without service.
I realize the Defence Research Board is working on this problem. Whether or not they are working in conjunction with other countries I do not know and I am not in a position to say. I do not know whether anyone in this committee can enlighten us in this regard.
However, Mr. Chairman, telecommunications is a subject which is under discussion at the moment. About one year ago I placed several questions on the order paper which at the time related to the C.B.C. These were prompted by a series of articles appearing in various papers across the country dealing with this problem in an exploratory fashion, providing information, and entreating the scientists of this country to experiment in this new area of communications. My opinion is that we should move very rapidly in this field.
I am aware of the fact that national defence communications are important and that the department is interested in this question. I am also aware from the information that
March 22. 1967

has been provided me that eventually we will attempt to send a satellite aloft to provide telecommunication for defence purposes only. However, this subject can also be related to other fields of communication essential to the country.
I am very conscious of this question of telecommunications because some areas of the part of the country that I represent have very little television service, some have no television service and some have bad television service. The people in these areas would appreciate the opportunity of being educated along with the rest of the country which have this facility made available to them.
Someone behind me says that perhaps we are lucky, but I suggest that with a satellite service perhaps we would be luckier in the sense that we would not be restricted to one particular program. We would not be subjected to what is at times the corruption of the C.B.C, though there are other times when their programs are good. I must say that my impression is that some of the programming is not too good; but regardless of the type of programming this is an area which requires urgent investigation.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
We must allow notional research or defence research boards, which have scientists trained in this field, to act. A few days ago the Prime Minister said that the Minister of Transport has the responsibility of co-ordinating work in this field. When talking with the minister I realized how unexplored the field is. We seem to be waiting to see what will develop. We have the technicians and the scientists to work in this field, and we have organizations such as Northern Electric and Bell Telephone which can be useful to us. We can create a vehicle to transmit messages, but we lack the capability of sending it into orbit. For this capability we must go to other nations. If the United States does not want to help us, or if it feels that our satellite may take up a spot in the heavens they might be interested in later, then we shall have to put up a satellite. In one sense we are at the mercy of countries such as the United States. At the moment I have no reason for believing they will not co-operate with us.
This capability is necessary for our defence, as well for the entire question of telecommunications. We must talk to nations other than the United States. Several have the capacity to send vehicles into orbit. From my
Supply-National Defence understanding of the problem, sending a vehicle into orbit does not require much more capacity than we now have. Nevertheless as satellites become more complicated they become heavier. We shall not have them in orbit for several years.
Our research at the moment is very limited. I understand that the attitude of our government is not to allow grants to those working in the research field in this sphere. I am thinking of the McGill University space research institute. It is essential, if we feel that communication between all parts of Canada is necessary, and if all parts of the country must participate in education, to consider carefully every aspect of this field. Whether they serve national defence or education, satellites are important. I do not know the technical problems, but I think that one satellite can transmit many messages simultaneously-telephone, television and radio messages, as well as others. In this area we should be more actively engaged than we are at present. More funds should be made available. Other countries are working rapidly in this field. If we wait patiently to see what will happen we might suddenly find another nation occupying that area we had thought to occupy in the first place.
We should have a vehicle to unite the north and south of our country, and to transmit from Vancouver to Halifax. It could transmit educational programs to our northern areas, where we are spending millions of dollars trying to provide an education for the inhabitants. The north is developing rapidly. When we think of the decline in the death rate, and increasing education among Indians, we must realize that our population will continue to grow. We must give our northern peoples an opportunity to see the rest of the country. We must show them that other parts of Canada welcome them. Only through this medium will they realize that. Once we provide those people with the opportunity to see the rest of the country, to see for themselves what exists beyond their own area of 50, 100, or 200 miles to either side of them, they will realize that they are part of the country. There can be no better way of spending money than on this type of research.
Item agreed to.

I should like to speak on this vote. The western end of the province of Nova Scotia is the area where the heaviest fishing is done, perhaps, in Canada, but we are still very short of the infra structure needed to maintain the growth of this industry, which is one of the mainstays of the province.

A large fish plant which has been expanding greatly in recent years-it is even going into whaling-is dependant on this wharf. I insist that steps be taken to correct this unfortunate situation. The Harbour at Meteghan River in Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare should be deepened, so that the shipbuilding plants can handle repairs of the draggers and other vessels which, as things are, must often waste time travelling long distances to undergo necessary repairs. I had reason to believe that such a ferry might be available because last winter when the Bluenose was placed to go into drydock for overhaul, the Leif Eiriksson, which is a car ferry, was supposed to relieve her. At that particular time, however, the Leif Eiriksson was required to relieve the M. V. Cabot and therefore was not available to replace the Bluenose. I presume that now, or at least by early summer the Cabot will be back in service, and therefore I urge the minister to consider putting the Leif Eiriksson, or some equally suitable vessel, into use as a supplementary service. It is absolutely essential that our tourist industry not be restricted; it should, rather, be given a very opportunity to expand.

Mr. Chairman, I have sat here for a number of hours, suffering with the minister, while he has laboured to explain these estimates and send them into the cold, hard world. I think this is an appropriate time to make a few remarks about our procedure of dealing with estimates. The minister I

am sure knows what I am going to say on this item, which includes the publication of estimates.
Perhaps I am preaching to the converted so far as the minister is concerned. It is his delinquent colleagues to whom I wish to address my remarks because they are delinquent through indolence, negligence or in attempting to slip these estimates through at the last minute.
The total amount involved in the supplementary estimates is $235 million and, if I may continue in the same vein in which I started, the period of gestation is all too short. These estimates were brought down on March 10, three weeks before the end of the fiscal year. The minister will likely say that this practice has been followed on many previous occasions, but in light of the fact that the estimates for the ensuing fiscal year show such a tremendous increase I do not think it is competent for us to let these supplementary estimates pass without registering a very strong objection.
It is a bad parliament that follows this practice. We have now no alternative because these estimates must be passed by the end of this month. It is an even worse government which brings down estimates at such a late date and indicates that the money has either been spent or committed. There have been problems but many of them have occurred because the government did not arrange its affairs as it should have by bringing these estimates down some 15 months ago. The government has gone forward, backward, sideways; it has wiggled, squirmed and jiggled like a go-go dancer with Saint Vitus dance. In my view this is not good enough.
I do not want to debate the reports of the standing committee on public accounts and on procedure, but we have attempted to deal with this problem. I hope we can go a step further. I mention this because the senior Minister without Portfolio made a speech the other day regarding procedure, in which he outlined what the government would like to see so far as the opposition is concerned. What the opposition wants to see so far as the government is concerned is some order in the way these estimates are brought down.
Some day I hope a fixed date will be set when the main estimates must be brought down, and a fixed date when supplementary estimates must be concluded in order that we will not have this situation occurring again and again. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the committee system, because I think it is time we gave our attention to it. The idea of having standing committees to which departmental estimates are referred is an excellent one, and an improvement of course in our procedures. But I raise with the minister, the government and the committee the question whether we have not gone too far along the lines of referring every department every year to a standing committee. This means that we have 24 standing committees. That is fine, but you cannot man 24 standing committees all meeting at the same time as the house and its committees are meeting.
I think we are suffering, as it were, from an excess of bad conscience. Because in the past we did not refer enough departments for committee scrutiny, we are now making up for it by referring too many all at the same t'me. I make this suggestion for the consideration of the committee of the whole and the standing committee. We now have 24 standing committees corresponding roughly to each department of government. Could we not, on the basis that the normal life of a parliament is four years, refer, say, six departments a year for detailed scrutiny by a committee? Then in four years you would have had every department of government studied exhaustively in a committee. But you would have in each year only six committees sitting, and it would be possible to man those six standing committees in terms of work of the members, the committees staffs, the translation service, and so on; whereas at the present time, while
1	think the desire is commendable, the work

March 22, 1967
Supply-Treasury Board is suffering and committees are not able to do the job because they lack the staff, and members lack the time they would like to devote to these matters.
I would therefore ask this committee of the whole, the government and the standing committee to consider the idea that instead of having every department referred every year we should have, say, six departments referred every year, so that in the life of an ordinary parliament you would have all departments given one thoroughgoing scrutiny in a standing committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just happened to come in at the appropriate time when someone was talking about the committee system of the House of Commons. I wish to add my protest in this respect. I think that the House of Commons has gone crazy over committees and the house itself has suffered accordingly. This is a committee of the House of Commons, a committee of the whole house, and should be used as it used to be used in days gone by, instead of hiving off small committees scattered all over the buildings on parliament hill.
You can be sure of maintaining a quorum in the committee of the whole house, but you cannot be sure of maintaining a quorum in some of our smaller committees. Time and time again we hear of committees meeting and waiting for a half an hour or longer for a quorum before they can proceed with their work. I say, Mr. Chairman, let us revert to half way between this system and the old, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Kamloops. Let this committee of the whole house deal with estimates to the fullest extent that is reasonable and from time to time refer estimates for more so-called detailed study by committees.
There is some advantage to this detailed study by committees once in a while, but not every year. Senior departmental officials have told me that burdensome as it is to appear before a house committee on estimates, nevertheless it is a spur and a help to them in their work because they are put on their mettle, they have to know their job and be able to answer the questions of interested members of the House of Commons. I would not subject them to this every year, but as the hon. member for Kamloops has quite properly said, perhaps six departments each year should be referred to our smaller committees. This system might very well satisfy the house.

As a matter of fact some years ago we had a committee on estimates. The idea with regard to that committee was just about what has been proposed by the hon. member. But I warn the House of Commons against the proliferation of committees. I have seen during the last two years the deterioration of the committee of the whole house and the House of Commons itself because hon. members have been occupied elsewhere. Of course the general public think we should be here in this chamber. For the last six weeks-and I am a fairly good attender in this chamber; I am either here in my seat or behind the curtains, and can generally be found-on the defence committee alone, with 23 other hon. members of this house. I have been attending twice and three times a day through the five sitting days of the week. Our only opportunity to be present in this chamber has been on the orders of the day. This is not right. Just think of the speeches the house has been deprived of hearing, because we have been absent on committee work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: What about the benefit to the defence committee?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
The defence committee has of course reaped the benefit. But a larger audience exists in this chamber. The present system is ruinous of the work of an hon. member; it is ruinous to the chamber itself and is putting too much emphasis on the committee system. The committee system has value, but its value is not as great as some outside observers maintain. Having done quite a bit of committee work over a great number of years, I come back to the point that here in this chamber more effective work generally is preformed.
There are special times and special investigations when better work is carried out by a smaller committee, but by and large this chamber is the place where the work should be carried out. I hope that instead of having 24 committees examining estimates, the bulk of the estimates will be covered here and the ministers concerned will stand up and disclose to us whether they know anything about the departments with which they are fumbling. We will soon find out. I support what has been said by the hon. members for Kamloops and others in regard to the committee system. It has gone too far too fast, and there should be a retraction in this respect.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word or two with regard to the committee system with which we have been experimenting during the last year or two. I think it has advantages in many ways, but I believe many of the advantages are lost because of bad scheduling. This is the point I particularly wish to make, namely that the committees should be set up early and the scheduling of the meetings of the committees should be such as not to interfere with the sittings of the house or with the sittings of other committees. During the 22 years I have been a member of the House of Commons I have been trying to put this point over in the various committees of which I have been a member, and in this chamber. However, I am sorry to say that there has never been very much in the way of material advance made in that regard.
If you have two or three committees authorized to sit at a certain time, they will almost invariably hold their meetings on Tuesday mornings and Thursday mornings, and if they are meeting more than twice a week they will probably all meet at the same time. I believe that many of the difficulties which the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has mentioned could be obviated by a reasonable scheduling by a house co-ordinating group.

It is the same as a bad debt in ordinary business. Remissions under section 22 of the Financial Administration Act are a different matter, where an indebtedness is forgiven.
